#3534. ‘Wild Horse Nine’ Review: Martin McDonagh’s Prickly but Unconvincing CIA Satire Recasts ‘In Bruges’ as the Stuff of a Classic Western

[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on September 3, 2026 during the 2026 Venice Film Festival. Searchlight Pictures will release it in theaters on Friday, November 6.]

Another melancholically splenetic Martin McDonagh jag about a banter-mad pair of murderers who go on a boys trip to purgatory (where they search their souls as they wait for death to find them), the prickly but unconvincing “Wild Horse Nine” strains to translate the post-Guy Ritchie bark of “In Bruges” into the language of a classic American Western. In this case, an American Western set on Easter Island and backdropped by Augusto Pinochet’s rise to power in the fall of 1973.  Related Stories ‘North of North’ Season 2 Review: Netflix’s Defiantly Nice Arctic Sitcom Is for the Warmhearted F**k-Ups ‘Hen’ Review: A Cockeyed Comedy Sees Europe’s Migrant Crisis Through the Eyes of a Chicken

McDonagh’s decision to recast his same old script against the backdrop of such a real and terrible event grants this new telling a welcome sense of scale, both in terms of its characters’ morality, as well as in regards to their greater place in history. But that decision is a double-edged sword that cuts the film off at the knees. Where “In Bruges” kicked off with the killing of a fictional altar boy, “Wild Horse Nine” is overshadowed by the deaths of thousands upon thousands of very real people, and that reality bleeds into the edges of the frame even when the seriocomic absurdity of McDonagh’s writing demands a world of pure invention.

Does the overlap make “Wild Horse Nine” feel glib? Yes, and thank god for that — if not for glibness the movie would lose the majority of its few solid laughs. The problem is that it also makes “Wild Horse Nine” feel as transparently manufactured as the CIA-backed overthrow of a foreign democracy. I can accept that an inexperienced hitman might have a dark night of the soul after shooting an innocent child during confession. By contrast, I struggle to believe that a veteran CIA agent who openly brags about his involvement in the Kennedy assassination would have a come-to-Jesus moment after orchestrating the demise of Salvador Allende. McDonagh has some good fun wrestling with whether or not we should care about such a mottled change of heart, but the point is gradually rendered moot in a movie whose emotions are less credible than its conspiracies.

The original Company man, Chris (John Malkovich, more locked in than he’s been on screen since “Burn After Reading”) is a natural hinge for the off-kilter comedy that McDonagh builds around him, in that he can be a joy to watch even when you don’t buy a word he’s saying. More than just an ordinary CIA agent, he’s the living personification of America’s efforts to destabilize foreign governments across the 20th century. He was close with Patrice Lumumba until the day the Congolese leader was executed by a firing squad. He was in Cuba to spur on the exiles who failed to overthrow Fidel Castro in 1961. He was even in Dallas, USA on a Friday afternoon in November 1963, doing things his ornery boss MJ (Steve Buscemi) would much prefer he didn’t tell you about.

He traveled to all of those places, and got all of those people killed, with the blithe imperiousness of a flag waving in the wind. Chris says that he’s killed 68 people over the course of his career, and he offers that information as easily as a rumor — in a way that makes it sound like the number could be half that, or double, and it wouldn’t make a difference.

Recently, fate has blown Chris and his office husband/platonic life partner/exasperated straightman Lee (McDonagh vet Sam Rockwell) down south to Chile, where the two of them have been hard at work orchestrating the September 11th coup against the democratically elected socialist president, knowing full well that it would plunge the country into decades of brutal dictatorship. Chris appears to delight in sowing chaos, and the fact that he gets to wear a cute little Panama hat while he does it only boosts his joie de vivre.

But Chris is fraying at the seams in ways that we can’t see at first — ways that will only begin to reveal themselves when he and Lee decide to celebrate their imminent success with a sightseeing trip to Easter Island, a short 2,300 miles off the Western coast of Santiago. There are still a couple of months to go before the coup, but the wheels are in motion, and there’s little for these men to do for now besides fly to Rapa Nui, look at the “big heads,” flirt with a couple of beautiful young leftists (the prissier but gentler of whom is played by “Ema” mega-talent Mariana di Girolamo), and mordantly reflect upon their role in the awfulness Pinochet will soon inflict upon his own people. That task is complicated and confused by the fact that Chris seems to be losing his memory, which casts Lee in the role of his peevish but loving caretaker.

“Wild Horse Nine” is only the second feature that’s ever been shot on the ultra-remote soil of Rapa Nui (Kevin Reynolds’ 1994 epic “Rapa Nui” is credited as the first), and McDonagh rightly exalts in the fact that he’s brought Hollywood to the end of the world. The first half of his movie largely adheres to the fiction that Chris and Lee are just on Easter Island to fuck around, which offers a semi-relaxed opportunity for us to take in the sights. Ben Davis’ sun-bleached cinematography renders the hills and beaches of Rapa Nui with the veneer of a lost idyll, the ancient moai statues assuming an especially sacred charge when contrasted against such profane characters.

Chris bemusedly laughs the statues off with ethnographic glee, mocking one of the shorter figures as a dwarf (in case the “In Bruges” déjà vu wasn’t already strong enough), but it’s clear that he’s shaken by the fact that some of them almost 750 years old. That they’ve stood there in silent tribute to Polynesia’s ancestors as empires rose and fell on faraway shores, each of them a graveyard of forgotten people just like him. By the same token, it’s similarly clear that he’s trying to get at something in his own mind as he and Lee listen to Judy Collins in their rental car, argue over whether or not any Nazis made it into heaven (among other even more aggressively screen-written subjects), and whisper sweet nothings to the wild horses that run about the island, but the specific nature of that something is hard for him to pin down.

Malkovich has the time of his life with that search for Chris’ last speck of humanity, which shines up from the bottom of his soul as his mind continues to erode. At once both insidiously relaxed and also choked with Catholic guilt, Malkovich’s performance marries the nonchalance of a cowboy to the paranoia of a bounty target. One minute he’s waxing poetic about dinosaurs, and the next he’s rigging his luggage with explosives (maybe) and checking the “Memento”-like reminder notes he’s slipped into his jacket pocket.

“Wild Horse Nine” loves Chris too much to pretend like we’re not supposed to, but Malkovich never asks for our sympathy because he knows that he’ll get it anyway, and not just because the purpose of Rockwell’s character is to ensure that we do. It’s Chris’ job to make rooting for the bad guys feel like the right choice. It’s the cornerstone of America’s post-war foreign policy.

So while Chris might be cut from the same cloth as John Wayne (to the extent that Monument Valley is revealed to be a place of great importance to him), his arc is aimed in the opposite direction of the one that Ethan Edwards traces across “The Searchers”; Chris is a major asshole this movie gradually puckers into a wayward hero, and while it’s all too easy to root for him to complete that transformation before time runs out, at no point does “Wild Horse Nine” sell us on the premise that it would mean anything in the end — even to him.

The movie, blessedly, isn’t Catholic enough to offer Chris a big moment of divine expiation; in lieu of building to a grand confession, he and Lee simply run afoul of their CIA higher-ups until their PTO turns into a matter of American national security. Guns are fired. Hostages are taken. The word “fuck” is used like a punctuation mark, and regrets are muttered into the wind long after there’s any way for them to matter.

It all gets a bit too busy and madcap as “Wild Horse Nine” — freighted with sadness during even its cheekiest bits, as is McDonagh’s way — scrambles to make up for the general listlessness of its first half. Never as funny as it is sardonic, and always reaching so hard to be more of both, the film’s most successful moments are mined from the ambient tension between memory and erasure.

Chris, we begin to suspect, would do anything to forget what he’s done, and his own mind is graciously willing to get him halfway there. The rest of the CIA will do anything it takes to make sure that Chris doesn’t share whatever it is that he still remembers. Surrounding them on all sides are statues that predated America by several hundred years, and will likely continue to watch over Rapa Nui long after our empire has been wiped away like a tear in the rain. In “Wild Horse Nine,” American interventionism is less effective as the set-up for some jokes than it is as their punchline.

“Wild Horse Nine” premiered at the 2026 Venice Film Festival. Searchlight Pictures will release it in theaters on Friday, November 6.

#3533. Jason Statham's 98-Minute James Bond-Esque Action Sequel Officially Hits Free Streaming

Jason Statham is a modern action movie star with a busy filmography spanning decades. He made his feature film debut in 1998 with Lock, Stock, and Two Smoking Barrels, where he played a small-time criminal called Bacon. Since then, he has starred in dozens of projects, from The Transporter and Crank to Fast & Furious Presents: Hobbs & Shaw.

Action movies are one of Statham's specialties. While some detractors may say his more recent movies are formulaic, fans of his work would agree that's part of the charm. To a certain extent, audiences know what they are getting with a Statham movie. Fans go in expecting to see him taking down scores of henchmen, looking cool while doing it, and that's precisely what they get.

Some of his newer movies arguably feel like they have 90s DNA. They are full of set pieces where Statham faces impossible odds against opponents with stormtrooper aim, and they are all the better for it. One movie that fits that description perfectly is 2016's Mechanic: Resurrection. Statham stars as Arthur Bishop. He's a mechanic, though, not in the traditional sense. Similar to The Beekeeper, his profession has a dual meaning. Bishop is actually a highly trained assassin, and he is called a Mechanic because he specializes in making his kills look like accidents.

Mechanic: Resurrection has many similarities to James Bond and spy thrillers. It's also currently available to stream for free on Tubi, with no subscription required.

Arthur Bishop may not work for MI6 with a license to kill, but he's been put in impossible situations only a special agent could escape. Bishop faked his own death at the end of The Mechanic, escaping to a quieter life. However, villains connected to his past saw through the facade. They then blackmail him into killing several high-profile targets, using his skills to make them look like accidents.

Bishop is forced to comply, as Crain (Sam Hazeldine) has taken Gina (Jessica Alba) hostage. Each kill in Mechanic: Resurrection is like a mini mission. Bishop must plan every hit with absolute precision and vanish without a trace. Like Bond, Bishop is resourceful. He sets up traps and takes down his enemies quietly, at least, until his cover is blown.

Bishop doesn't have Q Branch at his disposal, but he still relies on high-tech tools and gadgets to get the job done. Every kill takes place in a different environment, from a dingy prison to a secure high-rise building, and it's a treat to watch Bishop infiltrate each location while securing an escape route.

Mechanic: Resurrection starts where the original left off. The movie assumes you've watched the 2011 film, but it tells a solid standalone story that shouldn't leave audiences confused. As there's little backstory, Mechanic: Resurrection gets into the action almost immediately. It's a fast-paced movie, with many action set pieces crammed into its 98-minute runtime.

The 2016 movie has a satisfying conclusion, though it's a shame we never got a sequel. Mechanic: Resurrection performed well at the box office, grossing $125.7 million on a $40 million budget. It also outperformed the original. However, box office success doesn't guarantee a successful sequel. For example, Expend4bles was released in 2023 and took $51 million at the box office, a far cry from The Expendables 3's $209 million.

Without delving too deep into spoilers, Mechanic: Resurrection's ending offers a path to continue the story. However, it seems unlikely we will see Arthur Bishop return anytime soon. Jason Statham is working on multiple projects, including The Beekeeper 2, but there is no word of another Mechanic movie in the works. Still, Bishop's story has a good ending, even if we never get Mechanic 3, and you can enjoy Mechanic: Resurrection without worrying that it may lack a decent conclusion.

#3532. If You Loved 'East of Eden,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

One of the best things about truly great stories is how they can be endlessly adapted and reinterpreted. John Steinbeck published “East of Eden” in 1952, and each time it’s adapted to a screen, it looks a little different. Netflix’s try at this huge, complex story offers up some searing performances, especially from Florence Pugh as the notorious Cathy Ames. Ames is one of the best characters ever crafted in American literature, but her sociopathic nature has sometimes made her into a simple villain—but the series, and Pugh's performances, adds depth to the charcter. If the limited series has you wanting more complex female characters from classic novels, your next move is obvious: Vanity Fair, starring Reese Witherspoon as Becky Sharp.

First published in the mid-19th century, “Vanity Fair” by William Makepeace Thackeray is an enduring classic of American literature, satirizing the artificial manners and pretensions of Victorian society. At the center of the story is Becky Sharp, whose moral ambiguity and self-serving actions were surprising and unexpected at the time—and have made her a kind of antihero in the modern age. Sharp is a complicated character who, like Cathy Ames, can easily be flattened into a villain, a social climber who uses people.

The 2004 adaptation leans into the more modern take on Sharp’s character, giving her more justification for her actions and humanizing her more than the novel. Sharp is orphaned at a young age, but is almost feral in her determination to secure a position in society—which, at the time, meant securing an advantageous marriage. The story doesn’t have the same sweep as East of Eden, chronicling a relatively short period of time—but that period is the Napoleonic Wars, so there’s a lot going on. This gives the film a similarly epic feel even as it focuses on Sharp’s constant scheming and endless flirtations with people who she thinks can help her out.

In many ways, Sharp is simply playing by the rules imposed on her by men, and if that was scandalous in 1848, it’s almost heroic by today’s standards, and Reese Witherspoon imbues her Sharp with a bit of grace to reflect that. But she’s still someone who does what she must to survive and thrive, and that prickly edge will appeal to fans of Pugh in East of Eden. Rent Vanity Fair on Prime Video.

Need more historical epics with fascinating, complex characters? Luckily, the movies tend to specialize in that—here are a few more movies that fans of East of Eden will love.

If you thought the best thing about East of Eden was Florence Pugh, you’re going to love Lady Macbeth. Pugh plays Katherine, a young woman pushed into an arranged marriage with wealthy landowner Alexander Lester (Paul Hilton) in England in 1865. The marriage is solely intended to produce an heir, and Katherine is initially imprisoned in the house. When Alexander and his father leave Katherine alone for some time, she walks the estate and begins a brazen affair with a worker, setting off a chain of violent events that gets bleaker with each scene. Pugh’s portrayal of another dark, determined woman is mesmerizing. Stream Lady Macbeth on Kanopy or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

If you want more sprawling family drama in a historical setting, look no further than Legends of the Fall. Set in the early 20th century, it follows Colonel William Ludlow (Anthony Hopkins) and his sons Tristan (Brad Pitt), Alfred (Aidan Quinn), and Samuel (Henry Thomas) as they navigate life choices and deal with the emotional wounds they inflict on each other. From World War I to Prohibition, the Ludlows fall in love (sometimes with each other’s wives), suffer crushing loss, and remain connected to their ranch and the natural beauty of Montana through it all. Anchored by a star turn by Brad Pitt, this movie will scratch the itch left behind by East of Eden. Rent Legends of the Fall on Prime Video.

If you want to see a different take on the novel, check out the 1955 adaptation directed by Elia Kazan (grandfather of Zoe Kazan, who co-wrote and directed the 2026 series). Starring James Dean (who would die a few months after its release), it’s an old-school Hollywood epic that only covers the final third of the book. That makes it a very different narrative experience from the series, which has more room to explore the novel’s complexities—but the film looks amazing, Dean’s performance is terrific, and Kazan directs the heck out of it. Rent East of Eden on Prime Video.

Another choice for epic family drama, Giant was James Dean’s last film, and offers family drama in heaps. Like East of Eden, it follows a family over the course of decades as patriarch Jordan “Bick” Benedict, Jr. (Rock Hudson) tries to maintain his family’s ranching legacy in the face of changing times and a flood of oil money, while his former ranch hand Jett Rink (Dean) pines for Bick’s wife, Leslie (Elizabeth Taylor), and strikes it rich with oil. As money’s corrosive effect takes its toll on Jett, the Benedict family grows and changes, with plenty of drama to spare along the way. Rent Giant on Prime Video.

If East of Eden makes you curious about other adaptations of Steinbeck’s work, your next stop should be John Ford’s 1940 version of The Grapes of Wrath. Set during the Great Depression, it follows Tom Joad (Henry Fonda) after his release from prison for manslaughter. He finds his family has been forced off their land, and joins them in a desperate migration to California in hopes of finding work and security. Along the way, Joad kills again and undergoes what can only be described as radicalization, dedicating his life to organizing labor and fighting back against the predations of capitalist society. It’s a remarkable film pulsing with emotional heft and deep family drama, and if its story and setting are very different from East of Eden, the impact will be similar. Stream The Grapes of Wrath on Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

#3530. 10 Fun and Quirky iPhone Duo Apps Worth Checking Out

The launch of the iPhone Duo marks the first time that Apple has fundamentally changed the form factor of the iPhone. This is an exciting development because, among other reasons, it allows app developers to get even more creative. If you have an iPhone Duo, plan to get one, or if you're just interested in creative app interfaces, then you should take a look at these apps.

With Tiny Computers ($4), when you use the Duo half-open, it turns the bottom display into a keyboard, and the screen goes up top. The app features computers inspired by Commodore 64, Windows 95, iMac G3, Macintosh, IBM PC, Amiga 500, ThinkPad, iBook G3, Powerbook G4, and Windows XP. The attention to detail is great, but early App Store reviews mention that the app can be buggy.

I miss the tactile nature of playing music on my cassette player at home, and my old Sony Walkman clone. Deck-Man ($5) is an app that brings the Walkman's interface, complete with all the clicks and clacks, to your iPhone Duo. Each time you play an album, Deck-Man lets you "insert" the cassette in the player before it starts playing. The app links to your Apple Music account and it also supports playing local music files.

Foldissimo (free, $10 to unlock all songs) simulates the sound of airflow in an accordion as you fold and unfold your iPhone Duo. It has some songs pre-loaded, and you can pay $10 to unlock all songs. Foldissimo also supports a few other instruments (accordion organ, panpipes, and theremin), but you'll need to pay an additional $10 to unlock those.

With Flipcorder ($5), while the viewfinder and the retro interface are visible to you when you have the Duo in tablet mode, your subjects can also see the frame via the outer display. When you fold the Duo, the app saves the clip, and allows you to record up to 30 minutes of video per day, each of which is saved in a virtual "tape."

Orisuji ($5) is a puzzle game where you solve mazes by folding your iPhone Duo. It has 69 levels, and you'll be solving most of these by folding or unfolding the device to shift the position of the maze to make your characters move, unlock doors, or to find keys to get past locked doors.

Toastie ($3) is a game where you, well, make sandwiches: It has 10 recipes for you to master, with a time limit of 15 seconds per step as your in-game customers wait for you to serve them. You fold the phone to "cook" the sandwich; leave it folded for too long and you'll end up with burnt toast.

Marbles Unhinged (Free, $3/each to unlock all levels in a world) is a puzzle game where you guide a marble towards the exit in each level. When you fold your iPhone, it turns the top half of the level into a ramp, and alters the speed of the marble. You can keep the phone at different angles to change the nature of the stage, which will lead you to the solution.

ChompDuo (Free, $1 to unlock all monsters) uses the Duo's folding mechanics to make monsters "chomp" down, and you'll feel each bite via haptic vibrations. When you close the Duo, the monster's eyes stare at you from the outer display. It's a silly app that you or your kids could enjoy playing around with.

Unfold Your City (Free, $5 to unlock all cities) simulates pop-up books to guide you through the highlights of different cities. It reminds me of Robert Sabuda's beautiful pop-up books, especially when you use the app on iPhone Duo. It slowly pops up the artwork for each city as you unfold the device, and displays the cover when you close the "book."

In the Pokémon anime, the Pokédex is an encyclopedia that catalogs information about your friendly neighborhood pocket monsters. Dex Fold (Free, $3 to unlock optional features) simulates the device from the anime, which means that you can only use the app when you unfold the iPhone Duo.

Yellow Veil Pictures has boarded North American distribution rights for Callum Devlin‘s “The Weed Eaters,” a New Zealand cannibal horror film that notched a best feature win at SXSW Sydney in 2025. The indie banner is planning a winter release.

The deal for “The Weed Eaters” comes after the independent feature first debuted in the Unreleased Gems section of the Letterboxd Video Store, a video-on-demand streaming platform launched by the film-focused social media platform in 2025.

“‘The Weed Eaters’ exemplifies what we have come to expect from New Zealand indie films. It’s filled with heart and humor, but this one’s not afraid to get weird and gross along the way,” reads a statement from Yellow Veil.

Exact details on the release plan for “The Weed Eaters” went undisclosed, though Yellow Veil is primarily a digital distribution company with ventures into limited theatrical play.

“The Weed Eaters” follows four friends that have their holiday getaway upended when they stumble upon a strain of marijuana that makes tokers crave the taste of human flesh. #3528. John Ternus talks plans to improve Siri AI

During Apple’s quarterly earnings call, CEO John Ternus was asked repeatedly about Siri AI’s future. Here’s what he said about Apple’s plans for improving and expanding Siri AI.

Sometimes when Apple launches a new feature or product, the company sees its work as finished, and whatever ships goes unchanged for far too long. Many might characterize Siri this way, arguing the assistant went years without meaningful improvement or updates.

But according to Apple CEO John Ternus, the Siri AI that just shipped is only the beginning of what’s planned.

Yesterday on Apple’s quarterly earnings call, Ternus gave a rundown of Siri AI’s capabilities. He concluded: “We’re really excited to have rolled all these innovations out, and there’s still so much more we plan to do.”

This signals that Apple doesn’t see Siri AI as a feature that can now be left alone for a while. Instead, as we already saw in iOS 27.2 last week, Apple is focused on rapidly improving it.

Now that Siri AI is out, I would like to see it iterate as follows:

Support for a wider range of file types, such as PDF.

Accessing it from Search (especially on the Mac) should be instantaneous and reliable.

Proactively suggesting and reminding the user based on what it knows.

What are those future plans? It sounds like agentic capabilities may be among them. Ternus said:

With Siri AI, we really have the kind of—the Siri we always wanted. It’s primarily request-based today, but as we talked about at WWDC, it’s built on a modern, orchestrator-driven architecture that gives us real room to expand capabilities over time.

It’s telling that Ternus says Siri is “primarily request-based today” and mentions “room to expand capabilities” before pivoting to mention agentic features. It sounds like Apple is already, behind-the-scenes, envisioning and working toward a version of Siri that won’t need to be “primarily request-based.”

Finally, later in the call when discussing opportunities for services growth, including potentially launching new services, Ternus says: “We think intelligence is going to be another opportunity as well.” This refers back to an earlier discussion of Apple’s intent to charge a fee for expanded usage limits on certain Siri AI and Apple Intelligence capabilities. The idea is that as Siri evolves and improves, Apple will have opportunities to charge for certain features.

What are your takeaways from Ternus’s comments on Siri AI? Let us know in the comments.

#3527. Five Hacks Every Suunto Race 3S User Should Know

Suunto's new Race 3S is a lightweight, premium racing watch—but at a retail price of $599, it's a steep climb from the Race S, which is regularly on sale for $299. Still, there are certainly some major upgrades: The battery holds 46% more than the Race S's, and it's good for up to 38 hours of dual-band GPS; storage is double the Race S's, at 64GB. And as always, with the SuuntoPlus store, you can download apps and integrations so your watch can do more than just the default features. After all, the best way to justify the price is to really make use of everything the watch can do. Here are five ways to get more out of your Suunto Race 3S.

(Suunto Race 3S users should also check out these Suunto Run hacks).

There are several ways you can explore new hikes, straight from your watch or app, and all from the comfort of your home. First up, make sure you download offline maps at home. The Race 3S offers free worldwide offline maps with contour lines and place names, and you pay no subscription. Download your regions over wifi before you leave, so you aren't relying on a phone signal at the trailhead. The 64GB of storage leaves room for several regions, so grab the places you actually run, plus anywhere you're traveling. Menu paths can shift with firmware updates, so check the Suunto app if the layout has changed.

From there, build a library of points of interest. A POI is any spot worth returning to, such as a trailhead, water source, campsite, or viewpoint—and with Suunto specifically, you get a broad definition of “POI,” including spots for hunting, fishing, foraging, or wildlife watching. There are built-in POI types for noting where a deer seemed to have rubbed its antlers, where you've seen marine mammals, or where you've spotted mushrooms. And with the Race 3S, you can store up to 250 of them on the watch.

You can create them on the map in the Suunto app without even being there in person, or when you do stumble upon one, you can save your current location from the watch mid-run. You just have to plug in the POI as a Navigation Target under the options for your trail run or other activity. There's also a navigation app, accessible from the bottom of the widget list (select All Apps), and you can navigate without having an activity running. Organize them by area before a hiking trip, and you can navigate to a trailhead or a spring with a few taps, with the map showing the terrain around you.

For all the hikers out there, you can use Climb Guidance to preview the climbs. When you load a route, Climb Guidance splits it into flat, uphill, downhill, climb and descent sections, and shows remaining ascent. Use it to decide where to push and where to hold back. It doesn't set your pace for you, but it lets you pace by terrain.

Suunto’s Race line includes a storm alarm that watches for rapid pressure drops, a warning sign that weather is turning. It only helps if the barometer reading is trustworthy, so set your altitude to a known reference (a trailhead sign or a verified elevation) before you head up. To turn on storm alerts, go into Settings > System notifications > Alerts > Storm. (This is also where you can set up sunrise and sunset notifications.)

Just remember to recalibrate your barometer every time you start from a new elevation. Also under the Settings menu, you can select Alti & Baro, and then you have the option to either Set altitude or Auto adjust altitude. The auto-adjustment uses a GPS reading to make sure the altimeter is calibrated. But if you know your current altitude from a map, you can set it manually.

Training by heart rate is a great idea, but the default zones on your watch are based on broad formulas and guesses. With the SuuntoPlus app store, you can select Anaerobic Threshold and follow the instructions to find the heart rate where effort turns hard, so your zones reflect your body.

Be prepared: A threshold test is a tough workout. After a warm-up, you’ll be asked to run as fast as you can for 30 minutes. At the end, the app will tell you the heart rate that seems to correspond with your lactate threshold.

Now here’s the cool part: On your watch, go into Settings, then Training, then Intensity zones. Choose either the Default HR zones for all sports (what I’d recommend if you aren’t sure) or choose a sport under the advanced setting. Here, you can set the boundaries between your zones. The boundary at the bottom of zone 5 (and thus the top of zone 4) should be set to the number you got from the threshold test. If you’d like to tweak the other zones, Suunto has more information on how to calculate numbers for the other zone boundaries.

And for any threshold test, where precision matters most, I recommend pairing with a chest strap.

SuuntoPlus apps run on the watch and show extra data during activities, and these two are worth setting up during your training:

Cadence Coach shows live cadence and stride length so you can work on running form and, in Suunto's words, avoid injuries. Run a few easy sessions with it, find the cadence that feels smooth, and use it as a target.

Sprint automatically records your strides and sprints, using wrist acceleration. Instead of tapping laps during strides or hill sprints, just run, and review the efforts afterward.

Activate both in the Suunto app's SuuntoPlus store before starting an exercise, and watch your running economy start to improve.

My favorite time-saving shortcut is to pin the timer widget. Widgets are reachable from the watch face by swiping up or turning the crown, and you can choose which ones to show and in what order in the Suunto app. Move the timer to the top, and pin it so a crown press opens it. Then the upper button starts and stops the stopwatch, and the lower button resets it. It's ideal for intervals, cooking, and race-day warm-ups, and you never have to start a full workout for a quick timing job. The timer remembers whether you last used the stopwatch or the countdown.

Finally, I’m keeping my eye on the launch of the Race Planner feature. It's meant to build a pacing plan from your route, weather, and goal time, and then guide your pace on race day. Suunto hasn't announced a date yet, so I wouldn’t exactly buy the watch for it.

#3526. ‘Ghosts’ Fans Waiting for Season 6 Have the Perfect 5-Season Replacement on Prime Video

Taylor Vollman is a contributor at Collider. She has long quipped, “T.V. is my name, TV is my game.” Fortuitous initials aside, at the heart of a tired joke is a simple truth — she has a lifelong passion for television. And along with it, an affinity for movies, music and pop culture.

In a childhood time capsule, she had listed Friends, PB&J Otter, and Days of Our Lives among her favorite shows. But her tastes have not narrowed with age. Her viewing habits span TV Land classics, network hits, buzzy reality shows and streamer critical darlings.

Hoping to merge this passion with her love of writing, Taylor earned a bachelor’s in media arts and design with a minor in film studies from James Madison University. After working in marketing for years, she wanted to sharpen her skills and went on to graduate with a master’s in journalism from Georgetown University. Taylor has since pursued entertainment writing and reporting.

Rose McIver is no stranger to supernatural comedies. For years before she was communing with ghosts, the New Zealand actress was a crime-solving zombie on the aptly titled iZombie. Premiering in 2015, The CW series ran for five seasons, totaling 71 episodes. It recently found a new home on Prime Video. With its easy access, familiar face, and overlapping themes, it is the perfect show for fans of Ghosts as they bide their time until it returns for its regular season.

The CBS comedy follows Samantha “Sam” Arondekar (McIver) and her husband Jay (Utkarsh Ambudkar) as they transform their recently inherited Woodstone Manor into a bed-and-breakfast in upstate New York. But a head injury leaves Sam able to see and talk with the many ghosts already residing on the property. The network has pushed Ghosts’ upcoming Season 6 to its spring 2027 schedule, except for its holiday specials. The news comes after McIver revealed she will be absent from the start of the season, having recently welcomed her second child. But have no fear, the ghosts still have someone to talk to since Ben Feldman’s Kyle was promoted to a series regular. Ghosts recently aired its Halloween special on October 29, finally revealing Pete Marino’s (Richie Moriarty) fate after his Season 5 cliffhanger. It will also return with a two-episode “Ghostmas” special on December 10, 2026.

iZombie follows McIver as Olivia “Liv” Moore, a Seattle-based medical resident who becomes a zombie after an unfortunate boat party and subsequently upends her life. Keeping her newfound appetite a secret from nearly everyone, including her former fiancé Major Lilywhite (Robert Buckley), she goes to work in a morgue for unlimited access to brains. But a diet of brains comes with a side effect — Liv takes on the personality of the deceased and sees flashbacks to their life. Putting this newfound ability to good use, she pretends to be a psychic and partners with Detective Clive Babineaux (Malcolm Goodwin) to solve murders.

She soon finds a confidant in her boss Ravi Chakrabarti (Rahul Kohli), who makes it his mission to find a cure. Liv isn’t the only zombie in town, with the outbreak’s origin an early mystery within the series. David Anders’ Blaine DeBeers and Bryce Hodgson’s Donald "Don E." Eberhard run a brain-dealing syndicate to meet the dietary demands of its new population. The series manages to balance multiple genres — part comedy, part procedural, and part horror.

iZombie is based on the comic book series of the same name, created by Mike Allred and Chris Roberson. It was published by DC Comics’ Vertigo imprint. The CW tapped Diane Ruggiero-Wright and Veronica Mars creator Rob Thomas to adapt the story for the small screen. The series also stars Aly Michalka as Liv’s best friend Peyton Charles.

Woodstone is getting a reality TV takeover.

While a ghost-infested bed-and-breakfast and a zombie-infested Seattle don’t seem similar on paper, the series share more than just a leading lady. Ghosts and iZombie have a similar comedic sensibility, viewing subjects often seen in horror through an approachable lens and using humor to undercut their more grotesque elements. Ghosts uses crude phrases when approaching bigger afterlife themes, like getting “sucked off” to heaven or Alberta Haynes (Danielle Pinnock) declaring the evil Elias Woodstone (Matt Walsh) “went down on us” when dragged to hell. Similarly, iZombie leans into its comic book origins with its character and prop design. Liv just has a jagged haircut and pale complexion rather than a deformed face and slow-moving gait. The brains she eats even have a cartoonish quality, with the series interspersing Food Network-style cooking montages as Liv tries to add some variety to her all-brain diet.

McIver has made a career of hiding her supernatural abilities, often resulting in bumbling excuses and cringey results. While she isn’t solving actual crimes in Ghosts, she is often getting to the bottom of the ghosts’ many questions and familial mysteries. In either circumstance, Liv and Sam have unexplainable knowledge and the fibs they use as cover typically cause more hijinks. Plus, Liv has the added issue of a new personality every week, sometimes at odds with her petite appearance. One week she could be a Martini-drinking snob, the next embodying a frat boy, or even bursting into song while seeing through the eyes of an actress. Luckily, both characters have at least one confidant, iZombie’s Ravi and Ghosts’ Jay, who help cover her tracks even if they are then dragged along with her.

But more than comedy, both Ghosts and iZombie explore themes of reinvention, mainly through McIver’s characters. In Ghosts, she leaves behind most of her journalistic dreams to open a bed-and-breakfast. And with her new powers, she also prioritizes the happiness of her dead roommates. This new move pushes her to pursue other writing ventures she can accomplish at Woodstone Manor, like writing a book or screenplay. And while their aspirations are not the same, Liv leaves behind her picture-perfect dream of being a doctor and marrying Major. She instead finds new meaning in not only solving crimes but eventually helping other zombies.

Aside from its upcoming Christmas special, Ghosts fans have at least a couple of months until the CBS comedy returns with its regularly scheduled season. So, while they try to fill their time, iZombie is the perfect replacement with adjacent subject matter, familiar comedy, and manageable length. Plus, fans will also get to see the full extent of McIver’s acting chops on iZombie, as she essentially reinvents her character each week.

#3525. Iron Man Preps Fans For Civil War 3 With A Shocking Opponent

Twenty years after Civil War and ten years after Civil War II, Marvel teases a new conflict starring Iron Man. Iron Man’s psychological default is to mitigate risk, even at the cost of personal liberty. In the first Civil War, Tony Stark's guilt over disasters like Stamford drove him to become the bureaucratic enforcer of the Superhuman Registration Act, with a genuine belief that government oversight is the only way to keep the superhero community in check. In Civil War II, Iron Man clashed with Captain Marvel over predictive justice, as Stark’s mathematical mindset recognized that profiling the timeline based on unverified visions would be an attack on free will.

The conspicuous absence of another full-scale superhuman war since the catastrophic fallout of the second Civil War reflects collective maturity across a superhero community that realized these ideological purges only benefit their worst enemies. The tragedies of losing Captain America in the aftermath of the first Civil War and seeing Rhodey die in Civil War II taught Earth's protectors that internal warfare has fatal costs. The Avengers, Fantastic Four, and standalone vigilantes now proactively prioritize diplomatic channels to resolve internal disputes to prevent their pride from tearing their alliances apart.

Considering Iron Man is at the center of both conflicts, the most likely hero to launch a third rift among the Marvel Universe's superheroes is Tony Stark, especially when he's pushed to the limit by villains and allies alike.

Although Tony Stark is at the height of his superhero career's success following his mostly victorious encounters with villains like Madame Masque, the Whiplashes, and his former pupil Adam Ware, there's a growing concern about his future. Stark has been acting strangely, shifting his focus away from his own inventions and instead putting all his attention into the technology of others. Pepper Potts asks Reed Richards and Sue Storm to speak with Tony, and while they start on amicable terms, a particularly hotheaded Stark teases Reed Richards into a tense discussion about who could defeat whom.

One of the schemes Tony Stark mentions is the creation of a new Iron Man suit using Galactus' armor, which Mister Fantastic immediately shuts down.

After presenting the strategies they would use to defeat each other, Tony's girlfriend Luna Lucia leaves, leading Reed to apologize for the argument and admit he would never fight Iron Man. However, Tony Stark doubles down and tells Mister Fantastic that he would definitely win in a battle. With Happy Hogan's unexpected return, AIM's constant attacks, the events of The Infernal Hulk and Armageddon, and his time as the Incarcerated Iron Man adding more pressure, Tony Stark comes closer and closer to starting a new Civil War-like internal battle within the superhero community.

Although the Marvel Universe's heroes have spent several years proactively maintaining peace to avoid repeating past tragedies, the constant friction between mutant nation-states, superhero teams, and unauthorized vigilante groups creates an unstable foundation. Even the tightest alliances eventually break when an unpredictable tragedy forces heroes to choose between security and freedom, or between prevention and action. Earth's Mightiest Heroes continue to be caught off guard by villains like Varnae, Doctor Doom, and Red Hulk, and the world continues to be shaken by tragedies like the vampire takeover, Doctor Doom's dictatorship, and Red Hulk's attempt to launch World War III.

The Avengers have clashed and split up multiple times in Marvel Comics, and their inner conflicts have left permanent scars on the team.

Iron Man's past rivalries with Captain America and Captain Marvel pitted logic against pure morality and predictive military justice. Should a new conflict ignite, a clash between Mister Fantastic and Iron Man would be a war of competing hyper-intelligences, as teased by Reed Richards and Tony Stark's argument in Iron Man #11. Both super-geniuses are motivated by their compulsive need to solve the world's problems with the ambitious ideas they devise, but their methodologies are fundamentally opposed. Iron Man is focused on attacking threats head-on, saving as many people as possible with state-of-the-art engineering, whereas Mister Fantastic prefers less offensive strategies that exchange immediate results in favor of long-term safety.

Who do you think would win between Iron Man and Mister Fantastic?

#3524. Apple Wallet driver’s licenses coming to three new states soon

Apple Wallet driver’s licenses recently launched in Virginia and Oklahoma, but three more states are expected to follow soon, bringing us close to 20 US states on board.

Digital IDs are becoming far more common than they were when Apple first added support in the Wallet app back in 2021. And today, 16 US states plus Puerto Rico support the feature on iPhone.

The latest additions, Virginia and Oklahoma, debuted just in the last couple months.

And it looks like three more states will be coming soon:

This summer evidence was discovered of both Utah and Virginia being added to Apple’s backend for driver’s license support. Virginia has since gone live, so it’s expected that Utah will launch as one of the next supported states.

Kentucky previously announced it will support Apple Wallet driver’s licenses after upgrading its digital ID system this summer. All indications are that the upgrade has been completed, so based on the state’s original plans, we should see licenses in Apple Wallet soon.

North Carolina recently announced the launch of its new digital driver’s license system. As part of the announcement, it confirmed licenses will be supported in Apple Wallet by early 2027.

Additional states might always surprise us and launch in Wallet before Utah, Kentucky, or North Carolina. We’ve seen a clear acceleration of states signing on to offer Wallet driver’s licenses.

But for now at least, the three states above appear the strongest candidates to debut soon.

For more info on states that have pledged Apple Wallet support, see our coverage here.

Would you use an Apple Wallet driver’s license if it launched in your state? Are you using one already? Let us know how it’s going via the comments.

#3523. ‘La Bola Negra’ Wins Denver Film Festival Top Prize as More Regional Fests Boost Oscar Hopefuls

Regional film festivals matter to a movie’s more cosmic position in the awards season, even if it started somewhere like Venice, Toronto, Telluride, Cannes, or even Sundance. They generate excitement from real-world audiences (and often Oscar voters, as in Middleburg, Virginia), and they also help unspool headlines that keep films top of mind for those who follow the race.

The 49th Denver Film Festival, held in the hip, high-altitude Colorado city every year, just wrapped its annual event — which this year ran October 22 to November 1. Denver Film CEO Kevin Smith, artistic director Matthew Campbell, and their team brought out special guests including Carrie Coon, John Leguizamo, John Cho, D’Arcy Carden, Peter Gamble, Indya Moore, Hans Petter Moland, and more to receive prizes and be feted with special tributes. Several of these, including Coon for “The Liberation” and Leguizamo for “The Odyssey,” are in the awards mix. Overall, Denver showcased 130 films, including many awards season favorites. Related Stories ‘Wild Horse Nine’ Review: Martin McDonagh’s Prickly but Unconvincing CIA Satire Recasts ‘In Bruges’ as the Stuff of a Classic Western ‘Hen’ Review: A Cockeyed Comedy Sees Europe’s Migrant Crisis Through the Eyes of a Chicken

I served on the documentary jury this year and awarded the Maysles Brothers Award to one of the year’s most revered docs. We chose the nonfiction portrait of adolescence “Whispers in May,” winner of this year’s CPH:DOX and from Chinese filmmaker Dongnan Chen, which is still seeking distribution. Per our statement penned with Vanity Fair’s Chris Murphy and producer Justine Suzanne Jones as fellow jurors, it’s “a vivid and compassionate portrait of female friendship in the twilight of adolescence” and “formally daring and emotionally authentic.” Other films in the category included “Once Upon a Time in Harlem,” “Edward Said: Between Worlds,” “Rehearsals for a Revolution,” “Nuisance Bear,” and “SUMO: Spirit Weighs Nothing.”

Los Javis’ “La Bola Negra,” which just won the BFI London Film Festival audience award after winning that same prize at TIFF in September, won the Krzysztof Kieslowski Award for Best Feature Film. The Spanish epic about gay desire and Federico García Lorca is locked in for multiple Oscar nominations at this point, with its awards streak going back to Best Director at Cannes in May.

The Audience Award for narrative feature, just as it did at the Virginia Film Festival in October, went to Peter Farrelly’s Sly Stallone behind-the-scenes biopic “I Play Rocky.” The film, starring charming breakout Anthony Ippolito as the “Rocky” star/screenwriter, was the runner-up to “La Bola Negra” in Toronto’s audience award category. “I Play Rocky” is in select theaters Thursday ahead of a November 20 wide release, and its popularity as an audience favorite is proving hard to best at fests.

#3522. The Kindle Click Is the One Accessory Readers Have Been Waiting For

The Kindle is the world's most ubiquitous e-reader, but that's not the same as being the best. Don't get me wrong: Amazon deserves a large share of the credit for bringing e-books into the mainstream, and over the years, the Kindle has consistently offered a top-tier user experience, thanks to both generally good hardware and its integration into the retailer's ecosystem (for better or worse). But the company also rarely innovates in the space, waiting until other players like Barnes & Noble and Boox have tested out new features (like temperature-adjustable lighting and color screens, respectively) before adopting them itself. It's also not shy about dictating to customers what they can and can't do with their Kindles, from removing the ability to directly download copies of their e-books to limiting support for third-party accessories.

One such accessory has been maddeningly absent from the Kindle for years, despite the device having the technology in place to support it: a Bluetooth remote control (all Kindles released since 2018 support Bluetooth for connecting wireless headphones, but only wireless headphones).

A few years ago, third-party e-reader remotes became a big thing on BookTok, prompting competitors like Kobo and Boox to release their own versions of the peripherals. But with the Kindle's Bluetooth protocol locked down, Kindle owners were mostly out of luck; their only option a third-party clip-on accessory that attaches to the side of the device and manually taps the display at the press of a remote button—far from ideal, as they can only turn pages in one direction and block a portion of the screen.But finally, Amazon has seen the light and made its own Bluetooth remote, which it has dubbed the Kindle Click. More importantly, it has opened up the Bluetooth protocol within the Kindle firmware so it can connect to the accessory in the first place—though it will only work on Kindles from 2024 or later. (It pairs well with the new Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition, no pun intended.)

If you've never used one before, it can be a bit confusing to consider why someone would want a remote for their Kindle—why bother fussing with an extra device when you can just tap the screen or press a button? But for certain scenarios, it really does make sense.

Most practically, a remote can allow you to turn pages in circumstances where holding the e-reader itself is less than convenient, as when you're exercising: Holding a Kindle in your hands is tough when you're on an elliptical, and the words can bounce around too much if you're trying to use a spin bike while gulping down a few chapters of Yesteryear. But if you can prop the e-reader onto the machine's handlebars or a nearby surface, you can turn pages easily without missing a step.

Then there's the coziness factor: Reading under a big blanket in winter is one of the coziest activities I can imagine, but if you have to keep your arms outside of the blanket to turn pages on your Kindle, well, that's going to have an impact on how cozy you feel. (This is a real problem!) But what if you could comfortably arrange the device within your line of sight and turn pages while keeping your hands ensconced within your weighted throw? Some readers are willing to spend multiple tens of dollars to achieve this level of coziness.

How many dollars? In the case of the Kindle Click, around 35 of them (plus tax). Though that may seem like kind of a lot for a simple little remote with two basic functions and four buttons, it's just $5 more than the admittedly much cuter Boox Tappy. Speaking of which, while the new firmware update will also allow the Kindle to support cheaper third-party alternatives, there's no guarantee they will work as well.

So how does the Kindle Click work? Pretty seamlessly: You press and hold one button on the remote to put it in pairing mode. You open up the Settings menu on your 2024 or later Kindle and tap Accessories (you may need to perform a software update, if you aren't seeing that option). You tap Kindle Click in the resulting list to pair it. Once paired, the remote seems to connect to the Kindle automatically if the two devices are nearby and both powered up, provided you keep the latter's Bluetooth functionality turned on; you don't have to manually pair them every time.

That's pretty much it: Once you've opened a book, you can now turn pages with a button press (you can map which of the big grey buttons moves pages forward or back to suit your preferences). The volume-like buttons on the side can be used to adjust the brightness of the front light. You can't use the remote to navigate around the device or open a different book, so choose your reading material carefully before you enter your cocoon.

While the Click definitely works as advertised, Amazon could have been a bit more creative with its functionality. The Boox Tappy, for example, can switch between modes so it can be used to jump backward and forward between tracks in an audiobook or scroll pages in a web browser. While the Kindle can't display websites, it definitely supports audiobooks, but you can't use the Click to jump between chapters or adjust the volume while listening to an Audible book; these both seem like no-brainers to me.And while being able to turn the brightness up or down is nice, why not let the remote control the warmth settings as well, either through enabling different modes (like the Tappy) or via a combination of button presses? I'm not an engineer, so I don't know how complicated it would be to get that to work, but Amazon employs a lot of them, and I bet they could figure it out.

#3521. 10 Hacks Every Fitbit Edge User Should Know

The Fitbit Edge really hits a sweet spot for anyone who wants a minimalist fitness tracker but still wants a screen to tell the time and display workout data. Here are my tips on how to get the most out of it, including hidden features and surprising ways to use the device.

It’s not very obvious from the watch or the app, but you can switch watch faces—and if you use the app on your phone, you can change color schemes and sometimes even complications.

On the watch, long-press the middle of the watch face. This brings up a carousel of the faces you’ve selected in the app. The last screen in the carousel gives you a button to bring up the watch face library on your phone. This is the quickest way to open it, but you can also go to your device settings in the app.

From here, tap All Clocks and browse the available faces. Once you’ve installed a face you like, tap Customize to choose a color scheme and select which complications appear (like your steps for the day, or the weather). Sadly, the share button doesn’t seem to work—it sends a broken link to the old Fitbit website—but it’s a nice idea.

The Fitbit Edge is built with the assumption that you’ll want the side button on the right. But if you wear other jewelry or watches with it, or if you wear it low on your wrist and find that flexing your hand pushes the button, you can change this.

Just go into your device settings in the Google Health app, tap Device preferences, and then change Tracker orientation to put the button on the left instead of the right. This turns the display upside down, so take off your watch and turn it around so you can see it properly again.

The AI-powered Health Coach is both the best and the worst thing about the Google Health app. Fortunately, you can turn it off. What’s better, Google added a feature that lets you turn off the unprompted insights while still having the AI available when you need it.

Tap your profile picture in the app, then Google Health Settings, then Coaching, and select No Coach Insights. The chatty summaries (and notifications) will stop popping up throughout the day, but you can always hit the Ask Coach button if you have a question or if you want to use AI-powered food logging or workout logging.

The workout app on the Fitbit Edge is pretty minimal and can’t be customized, but it is possible to get more information during your workouts. Swipe down from the top of your Fitbit Edge screen, and tap the icon that looks like a wifi heart. This turns on heart-rate broadcasting.

Then go into the Strava app, hit Record to start a workout, and swipe up from the bottom of the screen to see workout options. Select the Fitbit Edge as your heart rate sensor, and now your phone can track your workout using heart rate data from the Fitbit. The Strava app gives you a lap button and can show you the time for your previous laps; it also shows you a map of where you are and where you’ve been.

Fitbit devices have always been a little over-enthusiastic about counting steps compared to other wearables, and they know it. Hand and arm movements can mistakenly contribute to your step count, but there’s a way to adjust the device’s sensitivity. If you wear the device on your dominant hand (say, on your right hand if you’re right-handed), go into Device preferences on the phone app and set your Wrist preference to dominant.

If you already wear the device on your non-dominant hand, you may still want to use this hack. Wear it on your left hand (if you’re right-handed) and still change your preference to dominant. This will tell the Fitbit to slightly undercount your steps.

The Fitbit Edge can use its own built-in GPS, or it can use the GPS that is built into your phone. By default, it will switch sources automatically based on what it thinks the best option will be.

But you can change this. Go into Device preferences again, and choose GPS settings. If you always carry your phone with you, and you’d prefer to save battery on your Fitbit, tell the device to always use your phone's GPS. On the other hand, if you want the Fitbit to handle its own GPS without piggybacking on your phone all the time, tell it to use the built-in GPS instead.

If your phone is an older one, switching to the built-in GPS will probably give you more accurate distance and pace than using the default switching. If your phone is newer, choose based on which device you want to preserve battery.

At the same time as the Fitbit Edge came out, Google made it so that the app can work with multiple Fitbits. If you sometimes like to have a screen on your wrist, but sometimes you don’t, you can swap seamlessly back and forth between the Edge and the Air (and a Pixel watch, should you happen to have one of those as well). No extra steps are necessary—just set up both of them, and wear whichever you feel like at any given moment.

Small screens can mean less visibility, but there is a setting that helps. In Device preferences, select Magnification and toggle it on. Now, triple-tapping the screen (three quick taps with one finger) enlarges what you’re looking at. You can use your finger to move the image around the screen to see different parts—for example, to get a better look at the number under the step count complication on some watch faces.

In this part of the app, you can also choose whether the magnification gesture gives you a 2x or a 3x zoom. To zoom out, just triple-tap the screen again.

The charger for the Fitbit Edge (like that for the Pixel Watch) is incredibly fast. If your watch is running low on charge and you don't have time to wait for it to charge, just put it on the charger for five minutes. Google says this gives it enough juice for a full day, and that matches my experience. Just now, three minutes of charging brought the device from 31% up to 41%.

If your Fitbit Edge tends to last about a week, you'll need about 15% to get through a full day. I like to use the always-on display (AOD), so I only get about three days per charge. If you're using the five-minute trick because you're low on battery, turn off the AOD if you have it enabled, and you'll get through the rest of the day. But if you always have the AOD enabled, you may be able to get into the habit of charging your Fitbit for about five minutes every day—maybe 10 every now and then—and never have to walk away from it for an hour like you would with most wearables.

I don’t follow the workouts the AI coach gives me, but it can be nice to have a record of what I did. So I’ll take a screenshot of my workout in Hevy, or a photo of my training journal, and show it to the Coach.

You can do this from the Ask Coach button in the bottom right corner of the app. Tell it which workout it should attach the exercises to (for example, “log this for my strength training session from last night”), and it will fill in the exercises in that workout summary. You can view past workouts in the Fitness tab.

#3520. iOS 27.2 adds two new features I’ve been really loving

iOS 27.2 arrived last week with a variety of new features and changes for iPhone. Here are two new iOS 27.2 features I’ve been loving lately.

I’ve used Apple Podcasts for the last few years after previously sticking with third-party apps. The native Podcasts app won me over with excellent features like transcripts and automatic chapters.

My main hesitation in recommending the Podcasts app, however, has been its confusing Up Next queue. Thankfully, iOS 27.2 delivers a long-awaited fix.

In iOS 27.2, the Home tab in Apple Podcasts splits Up Next into two separate sections: New Episodes and Continue Playing.

These new sections offer, in my view, a much better system than what was there before. I no longer lose track of episodes I’ve previously started, since they’re not getting replaced by new episodes in my queue. Instead, there’s a clear divide between what’s new and what’s in-progress.

Shared Albums have long been one of my favorite features in Apple Photos. I don’t post on social media often, but I do love sharing photos and videos with close family and friends via the Photos app.

iOS 27 brought big upgrades to Shared Albums, the first notable changes in years. And to my surprise, Apple has already introduced even more improvements with iOS 27.2. Per Apple:

Shared Albums in Photos adds the ability to edit captions and comments, to avoid adding duplicate photos, and can display a reminder before albums expire so participants can save important photos and videos

Support for editing captions and comments is long overdue, but a welcome addition. I also love the prompt that helps prevent duplicate photos, because I always find myself needing to double-check if I’ve shared certain photos already—now I don’t have to anymore.

#3519. ‘Everytime’ Review: Sandra Wollner’s Infinitely Beguiling Portrait of Grief in the Digital Age Is One of the Most Haunting Films of the Decade

[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on September 10, 2026 during the 2026 Toronto International Film Festival. 1-2 Special will release the film in limited theaters Friday, November 6, with a wide release to come in February 2027.]

I don’t believe in an afterlife, but that’s OK because the people I love most are never going to die. Not to me. At least, not in the way they used to before our species began to migrate online, to store our memories in the cloud, and to digitally encode the raw data of our existence onto everything we touch.

My father was born in 1939, the same year that Iowa State College scientists John Vincent Atanasoff and Clifford Berry built the prototype for the first binary-based computer; in the months after he died 75 years later, I often felt the reflex to reach down and call him from the iPhone that fit inside my pocket. To ask if he’d seen the Rangers game, or to tell him that I’d gotten engaged. I knew that he was gone, of course, but the piece of consumer technology I’d used to connect with him when he was alive had created a separate neural pathway between my brain and his being — a crude one-way network that didn’t begin to break down until much later in my grieving process.  Related Stories I Remember ‘Rocky’: My Front Row Seat to the Marketing of a Million-to-One Blockbuster MUBI Has Cleared the Path for Sandra Hüller to Land Multiple Oscar Nominations This Season

A decade later, those pathways have grown exponentially more complicated and convincing. The emergence of AI has led to a variety of ghoulish attempts at deathlessness and resurrection (from bots that feed on your grandma’s Facebook data to the ChatGPT Theodore Roosevelt who Trump was “honored to be with today” at the former’s Presidential Library), but such products and publicity stunts miss the fact that everyone is already being (temporarily) immortalized on a server farm somewhere, the traces of our existence shed into the digital ether like a Pollock-like splotch of invisible ink.

Charlie Kirk’s face is Twitter’s most ubiquitous meme. My long-deceased college friend you’ve never heard of sends me hacked emails full of links to “old pictures they found of us together.” The cancer-stricken hedgehog I fostered for a few months in 2016 still cycles onto my home screen at random sometimes, and he’s now been buried behind a house in suburban New Jersey for longer than he was ever alive. People have always looked for errant glimmers of the dead in the world around them, but now the past runs parallel to — imprints upon, and circles around — the present to a degree that can severely confuse the relationship between the two.

Sandra Wollner doesn’t believe in an afterlife either, but she’s certainly attuned to the mysteries of this one. Picking up where the equally spectral likes of “Personal Shopper” and “Aftersun” left up, the Austrian writer/director’s mystical and magnificently beguiling “Everytime” takes a rather ambivalent stance towards what happens when people die these days, or at least — per its curious title — towards how we mourn them from inside the flat circle of a temporal overlap where yesterday and tomorrow are folded into the pockets of an ever-expanding now.

There are no clear answers to be found in this astonishing third feature, which shares a number of thematic similarities with Wollner’s “The Trouble with Being Born,” but retains one crucial difference (that film, about a man who has an implied sexual relationship with a child-sized android coded with the memories of his missing 10-year-old daughter, unsurprisingly had trouble securing American distribution). Indeed, the grounded portraiture of the movie’s first 70 minutes eventually gives way to a final act so cosmic and surreal that it becomes all but impossible to pinpoint the precise location of Wollner’s characters in space-time; to say for certain whether “Everytime” has glitched into another dimension, or if it has invited another dimension to glitch into our own. Initially timeless in its nuanced and deeply recognizable depiction of loss, and then even more so as it gets devoured by the meta-modern flourishes that have fringed its story from the start, this is perhaps the most forward-thinking film I’ve ever seen about the changing face of grief.

The premise couldn’t be simpler, though Wollner’s incredible prologue — a careful arrangement of low-event long takes that emphasize how people move through spaces in time — trains our eyes to privilege texture over incident. While there’s little to distinguish single mother Ella (“Everyone Else” star Brigit Minichmayr) and her children from any of the other families strolling through the soft orange haze of a summer afternoon in Berlin, our senses pick up on the uneasy tension between the watchfulness of Gregory Oke’s 35mm camera work and the vivid intensity of the film’s sound design (it’s worth noting that Oke also shot “Aftersun”). The voices are close, but the bodies far away. Teenage Jessie (Carla Hüttermann) turns her head to look at an unseen pop as her family walks home through their local metro station, but we don’t think much of it at the moment. It’s probably nothing. And yet, I suppose it could be anything.

At the very least, that sharp noise is enough to suggest that the film’s environments may not be as benign as they seem, and a silent but soon unbearable tension starts to mount as the day wears on. As Jessie’s boyfriend Lux (Tristán López) comes over to hang out while her kid sister Melli (Lotte Shirin Keiling) annoys the shit out of her by banging on a keyboard; as Ella cooks dinner; as Jessie plays “Minecraft” late into the night on an island bathed in the light of a sinking square sun.

Later, in the waning hours before Jessie’s family is due to leave for a holiday in Tenerife (where she once vacationed as a toddler), Jessie and Lux will sneak out to a dance club, take a few pills, and watch the next day begin from their perch atop the roof of an apartment building. He will note that he’s recently noticed a strange number of seagulls in Berlin, and then fall asleep. She will stand up to film one of them flying past on her iPhone, and then — in one of the most arresting screen images in recent memory, a vertiginous collision of everything and nothing all at once — she will fall off the edge of the building to her death. The city doesn’t notice. The camera scans the treetops. The euphoric synth-pop of David Schweighart’s score kicks in as we suddenly begin to soar through the skies of Jessie’s “Minecraft” world, eventually plunging down through the dirt and into the unrendered levels of code below.

From there, “Everytime” settles into a crushingly quotidian register. Months have passed, and everyone is doing what they can to move on with their lives. Ella takes work calls while visiting her daughter’s grave, while the stoic young Melli texts life updates and other messages to her dead sister’s phone (she’s big on emojis). But things are not as settled as they seem, and Lux’s return from a semester abroad forces Ella and Melli into a more direct confrontation with Jessie’s memory — with the unresolved feelings she left behind. The girls keep running into Lux (and to his nice new girlfriend) around town, and soon begin spending time with him on purpose. They are bound together not only by their shared grief, but also by the unspoken guilt and blame that Lux and Ella can only hope to expiate through each other.

While Jessie is seldom mentioned by name, the bizarre mutual reliance between a middle-aged woman and her dead teenage daughter’s former boyfriend makes her the subject of every scene (much to the annoyance of people who would prefer to compartmentalize the pain of her loss). Jessie is the reason why Ella and Melli attend Lux’s birthday party; Jessie is the reason why Lux joins Ella for a tense lunch at her ex-husband’s house, and why he begins sleeping over at her apartment.

But these domestic frictions are — largely, but not merely — a means to an end so far as Wollner is concerned, as her film leverages them to focus on a series of increasingly abstract phenomena. Jessie is certainly the reason why each of the locations we saw her walk through before her death feels haunted when “Everytime” revisits them, but could she also be the reason why the shadow that falls across her bedroom at night appears to resemble a polygonal cube? Why a seemingly pilotless drone shows up to beckon Ella into a pitch-black parking garage? Why the dead girl’s computer glows with an unnatural brightness whenever the lights turn off?

Wollner’s characters never ask such questions aloud, but she poses them to all three of her leads in a way that compels them to look for signs in the digital detritus that Jessie left behind. Lux is drawn back to the old pictures and voice notes on his phone, while Mille stares at the WhatsApp chat with her sister as if waiting for a response. These signs complement, but never overwhelm, Wollner’s attention to the analog poetry of the natural world — to the shimmer along the surface of a lake, or the sound of the wind rustling through the trees in the woods where Jessie and Lux got high on her last night.

It’s easy to imagine a version of this film that more explicitly addressed how digital technology is transforming how we mourn the dead, but Wollner would rather plumb the mysteries of the present than speculate about the answers of the future; the portals between worlds have already been ripped open, and will only begin to lose their power as they get labeled and branded.

Eventually, Ella makes the spontaneous decision to bring Mille and Lux to Tenerife for the trip they never got to take. That’s where things get weird, and the math of the universe starts to contradict itself. It would be a terrible disservice to reveal anything specific about what happens next (and so I won’t), but the extraordinary magic trick that “Everytime” pulls off in its final stretch is rooted less in incident than in execution.

Its ineffable power belongs to how matter-of-factly Wollner tears apart the fabric of her film’s reality at the same time as she threads it together, and how the look on Minichmayr’s slacken face — her restrained but masterful performance a wonder of tightly bottled pain and lingering disbelief — reconciles those opposite energies with the instinctive naturalness of a mother’s love. It also belongs to the almost unquestioning acceptance that Keiling endows within Melli, the young actor’s posture embodying how this movie teeters on the precipice between a child-like vision of the world (soft and malleable) and the more hardened sense of reality that arrives with adulthood.

Wollner may not trace the character’s arc in the legible terms of a typical coming-of-age story, but Melli experiences a remarkable transformation over the course of the film, her petulant first line (“You always leave your stuff lying around!”) assuming an unforeseeable new context by the time we arrive at her closing narration.

As a medium born from — and once dependent upon smoothing over — the friction between stillness and movement, stasis and change, cinema has always been uniquely adept at conveying the radical effect that technology can exert on how we perceive time and space in the world around us. The switch from celluloid to computer chips saw the movies transform from an illusory art form to a representative one, at the great and continued risk of forfeiting its original power. Engaging in a thrilling and increasingly contested negotiation between 35mm film stock and crude DV video formats, “Everytime” pulls at that tug-of-war from both ends until the uncertain space at the center grows large enough to sail through, and still enough to hang like a painting in the sky.

I am now a father myself, the parent of two young kids whose faces sometimes remind me of my own dad in the same tactile way that people have been survived by their children since before the invention of the wheel. We keep a framed 4×6 photograph of him with a cigar in his mouth on the Blu-ray shelf in our living room, and I sometimes catch my kids talking about it as if the picture itself were their grandfather, rather than just a capture of his likeness. Ask my six-year-old to draw a self-portrait and he’ll sketch you the image of his Roblox avatar. If I ever were to lose him, I wonder how long it would take my nervous system to process that he was gone.

Like many 21st century parents, my wife and I take photos and videos of our kids throughout the day without thinking, and — after wrestling them to bed at night in an exasperating forever war of attrition — we invariably scroll through our phones and take stock of their cuteness in peace. Stills, videos, stickers, and more, these two-dimensional images, I sometimes feel with an uncertain pang of dismay, are our real children. The versions of them we commit to memory. The after images we see in our dreams. They are the kids we mourn as our son and daughter eagerly outgrow their current models every time you look away for too long, and the ones we would cling to in the unthinkable event that either of them disappeared from this mortal coil before we did.

And so, Wollner’s staggering new film suggests with a tender but uneasy twinkle in its eye, we’ve gradually steeped ourselves in a world that guarantees they never will. How strange and unnatural is that? Compared to the alternative, I fear it may not feel that strange or unnatural at all.

“Everytime” is screening at the 2026 Toronto International Film Festival. 1-2 Special will release it in theaters in the United States.
