#3494. Why Those Flashy Halloween Contacts Are a Bad Idea

Contacts with cat pupils or neon colors can be fun, but are you sure you want to put a piece of plastic from a costume store into your eye? Experts, like those at the American Academy of Ophthalmology, warn against it. These non-prescription contacts are technically illegal in the U.S. (even though plenty of companies sell them anyway). The CDC warns that the risks include "eye sores and vision loss."

Cheap Halloween contacts tend to be one-size-fits-all, but the AAO points out that contacts should never be one-size-fits-all. A contact that is too large or too small for your eye can cause corneal abrasions, corneal ulcers, and can result in infections like keratitis. Infections can, in severe cases, lead to blindness. A 2017 report from the FDA found bacterial contamination in 27% of costume contacts.

If you do wear contacts (Halloween or otherwise), the AAO recommends keeping an eye out for symptoms like redness, swelling, pain, or excessive discharge. Seek care as soon as you suspect an infection. Your eyes are more sensitive to infections than other parts of the body, so be cautious.

Legally, contacts require a prescription, so if those colored contacts you're eyeing can be bought without showing a doctor’s prescription, they’re not legit. The real thing can be expensive, though: I found prices of $40 and up from lens.com, Discount Contacts, and Wicked Eyez.

These websites all let you order online, but you’ll have to provide your prescription information before you can check out. Fortunately, the Federal Trade Commission has ruled that providers must give you your contact prescription after a fitting so that you can take the prescription elsewhere. And they cannot charge you extra for this.

Once you’ve got the lenses, you have to know how to take care of them. If you wear contacts every day, you already know the drill. But if you’re just picking up a pair to use with a costume, here are the basics:

Wash your hands before handling the lenses.

Store them in contact lens solution, and keep the lenses and their case clean.

And for Pete’s sake, don’t share them with your friends!

Just remember, the bloodshot look stops being cool after you take your zombie costume off.

#3493. iOS 27.3 and macOS 27.3 add Vertical Tabs, Adaptive Dark Mode, and more to Safari

Apple just released the first betas of iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, and macOS 27.3, with some big changes to Safari. The updates add a new vertical tab layout, Adaptive Dark Mode, and Siri AI Custom Actions.

Safari in iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, and macOS 27.3 is adding a new Vertical Tabs design option. If you choose this design, you’ll see your tabs arranged vertically along the left-hand side of Safari rather than along the top, as in the traditional Safari design.

By default, Vertical Tabs show as icons in order to maximize vertical and horizontal space. If you’d like, you can also resize the tab bar to see website titles.

To try Vertical Tabs in the new iOS 27.3 beta, head to the Settings app, choose Apps, tap Safari, then look for the new Vertical Tabs option. On Mac and iPad, the feature can also be enabled via the “View” menu in the Safari app directly.

Vertical tab layouts have become an increasingly popular web browser feature. Arc from The Browser Company popularized the option. Arc, however, ceased development last year, and The Browser Company announced last month that it will discontinue it altogether in December.

If you regularly visit a website that doesn’t support Dark Mode, Apple’s next round of software updates adds Adaptive Dark Mode. This will automatically apply Dark Mode to websites that don’t support the feature.

If Dark Mode is enabled on your iPhone, iPad, or Mac and you visit a website that doesn’t support it, you’ll see a new “Try” button. If you tap this, Safari will automatically create a Dark Mode version of the website.

You can choose to have Adaptive Dark Mode automatically kick in or use it on a site-by-site basis.

Finally, Siri AI can now take direct action on tabs in iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, and macOS 27.3. This includes things like using Siri to move, sort, organize, and close your tabs.

In a future update, Siri’s on-screen awareness will also expand to include the entire content of a website, not just what’s visible on the screen at a particular moment.

iOS 27.3, macOS 27.3, and iPadOS 27.3 are rolling out to developers for beta testing today. The update will likely be released to everyone sometime in December. What do you think of these new Safari features? Will you try out the new Vertical Tabs feature? Let us know down in the comments.

A beloved Chicago Fire star has addressed his exit from the show after being featured in 300 episodes of the series.

Since premiering on October 10, 2012, the drama series has reached its 15th season, which is an impressive feat. That also allowed the series to produce a landmark episode. And it was a massive draw as reviews of Chicago Fire episode 300 spread online as soon as it aired. Of course, much of that discussion centered on one thing: the fact that longtime series star Joe Miñoso left the show.

As viewers have been discussing Cruz's exit, Miñoso joined the discussion during a recent TVLine interview. While talking to the outlet, the popular actor was asked to explain what led to him leaving the show after so many years. In response, he noted that even though he didn't ask to be written off the show, he agreed with the creative decision. Check out Miñoso's comments below:

I will say, at the same time, there was something in me that felt it was time to move on. We had done so much with the character. I remember thinking about it a lot midseason [during Season 14], just because we had explored so much. And when we got the twins storyline, I was like, "This feels like the right time." So the news came my way, but I understood it, and they were so gracious.

After Cruz spent years as one of the most likable Chicago Fire characters, it is hard to see him go. However, that doesn't mean that the actor's association with the NBC drama is over. Instead, Miñoso told TVLine that he'd been asked to come back to direct episodes of the series.

Literally on the heels of that, I got asked if I was interested in still directing [episodes of the show], so it was real whiplash. And since then, it's been a journey into the world of this show in a really different way. I've had the great pleasure of shadowing a bunch of really amazing directors, and seeing what they do in that front office, which we don't get to see enough as performers. Those people are working their butts off so much every day, and it gave me more joy toward the process.

Anytime a longtime character leaves a show, observers typically focus on how they are written off. In Cruz's case, he was given a multi-episode arc focused on putting his family first after an injury and the birth of his twins. When asked about the storyline, Miñoso told the outlet how thankful he was for how his character's decision to leave the firehouse was handled.

I thought it was wonderful. We really haven't had the opportunity so much to see the dark soul moment for a character on this show, and seeing whether or not he can bring himself out of it. What's beautiful about it is of course it's all tied into the firehouse family and the hope that they bring him. I considered it an honor and a joy, and I thank them for trusting me with the material. That was some really intense stuff that they gave me to do, and I love them for it.

As anyone who has watched the ups and downs that Chicago Fire's characters have gone through can attest, the series has included some devastating moments. As it turns out, Cruz could have become the focus of another heartbreaking turn, as Miñoso told TVLine that his character's death was considered by the series' showrunner. Ultimately, however, the show's bosses thought that would be too sad.

While not going down that route saved viewers some despair, Miñoso told the outlet that leaving the show left him in tears for days. "I was crying for a week straight. And I thought I got a lot of that out of my system during the hiatus, but no, it was highly emotional."

For people who have watched Chicago Fire since the start, it will be strange to experience the show without Cruz. Still, as the One Chicago franchise has proven time and time again, one character disappearing is always a massive opportunity for other figures to step up. It will be fascinating to see what will happen now that a major hole has been left behind.

Chicago Fire airs Wednesdays at 9:00 p.m. ET/PT on NBC and streams the next day on Peacock.

#3491. One of the Best QLED TVs of 2026 Is Over $1,300 Off Right Now

TCL has been pushing the boundaries of QLED TVs, making some of the best in the market at very competitive prices. This year, the company released its QM8L model, introducing a new design and impressive features and specs to a series that isn't even their flagship. Right now, the 65-inch QM8L is $1,197.99 (originally $2,499.99), $100 cheaper than it was just earlier this month, reaching its lowest price since it launched in April, according to price-tracking tools. Larger sizes are also seeing substantial discounts.

One of the first things you'll notice about the QM8L is the “Zero Border” bezel design, which gives it a modern, minimalistic look. When you turn it on, you'll likely note how bright this TV gets, which is a huge advantage QLEDs have over OLEDs. TCL claims it reaches 6,000 nits—seeing as the brightest OLED TV on the market only reaches 700 nits, no OLED can come close to this unit's brightness. Another important spec to note here is the local dimming zones: TCL claims this TV has up to 4,000, which means it gets top-tier backlight control, limited light blooming (thanks in part to TCL's "Halo Control"), and incredible contrast levels that some might not be able to distinguish from an OLED.

As many of us won't manually calibrate our TVs, the picture modes you can switch to in the settings will be most people's go-to. This TV's "Filmmaker mode" provides accurate color and picture, and if you're a gamer, you can use the native 144Hz high-refresh rate. If you don't already have a surround sound system at home and want to keep a minimalist setup, the QM8L comes with Dolby Atmos-ready Bang & Olufsen speakers, which offer above-average audio output compared to most TVs. You can read more about these features in CNET's 8.8/10 review. If 65 inches isn't quite right for your home theater setup, take a look at the QM8L's other sizes, which are also discounted right now.

#3490. Netflix's 'Haunted Hotel' Just Broke a Major Streaming Curse

Jeffrey is a freelance features writer at Collider. He is an MPA-accredited entertainment journalist and a Tomatometer-approved critic based in the LA area. He graduated from the University of Texas at Austin with a Bachelor of Science in Radio, TV, & Film and a Bachelor of Arts in Theater.

Editor's note: The below contains minor spoilers for Haunted Hotel Season 2.Netflix's breakout animated hit, Haunted Hotel, has just wrapped up its second season. While the series first premiered to little fanfare last year, it's now building momentum and a sizable organic fanbase. With the news that the show has officially been renewed for Season 3 — right before Halloween, no less — Haunted Hotel just broke a streaming curse that's killed many promising shows in the past.

Over the past several years, some of Netflix's buzziest shows have debuted, garnered a sizable following, and were then suddenly and unceremoniously cancelled, leaving viewers on a huge cliffhanger. One of the streamer's biggest casualties was the animated series Inside Job, which was renewed for a second season in June 2022. Six months later, creator Shion Takeuchi revealed that Netflix had cancelled the series, rescinding the initial renewal.

The show has already been renewed for Season 2!

Thankfully, Haunted Hotel hasn't suffered the same fate as Inside Job, Sense8, The Boroughs, and so many other great Netflix shows that were cancelled before their respective stories could reach a proper conclusion. This Season 3 renewal likely comes as a big relief to the show's dedicated fanbase, who have been creating their own art and video edits. More than that, the announcement that Haunted Hotel will return for another season emphasizes the power of the show, world, and characters Matt Roller has created.

Haunted Hotel follows the Freeling family, who run the Undervale Hotel that single mom Katherine (Eliza Coupe) has inherited from her late brother, Nathan (Will Forte). Joined by her kids, the devious Esther (Natalie Palamides) and the studious Ben (Skyler Gisondo), Katherine tries to make the best of the family's situation and save their failing hotel. However, the Undervale is actually haunted by hundreds of ghosts — including Nathan, whom everyone can see. Dealing with the hotel's spectral residents is no walk in the park, and hijinks ensue.

Four franchises, four completely different ways of getting underneath your skin. This is the one built out of your particular fear, why it works so well on you, and what it would leave behind.

Your nightmare does not wait outside the door. It waits for you to close your eyes, which you are going to have to do eventually, because nobody has ever won that particular argument.

Your nightmare is not really the doll. It is the face of the person you tell, and the way they decide, very kindly, that you have imagined all of it.

Your nightmare has your number, knows your name, and has almost certainly been inside your house before. The worst part is that you already know them.

Your nightmare is not really about you. It is about the people asleep down the hall, and the feeling that whatever is here is not interested in leaving.

Haunted Hotel lovingly parodies the horror genre and its many subgenres while also telling a surprisingly poignant story about a struggling family picking up the pieces and trying to move forward in their lives. While Season 1 builds to a shocking yet organic reveal about Nathan's death that belies his optimistic personality, the series also highlights the wonderfully weird and endearing friendship between Esther and Abaddon (Jimmi Simpson), an immortal and mischievous demon now cursed to wander the Earth in powerless human form. Abaddon essentially becomes the Freelings' unofficially adopted child, and his storyline pays off with one fantastic Season 2 episode.

While Haunted Hotel's animation is much more vibrant, elaborate, and exciting in Season 2, one episode in particular cements the Netflix series as an animated masterpiece. "Ghost Day Out" involves the Undervale's ghosts breaking out of the confines of the hotel due to the strength of a once-in-a-generation full moon. Finally able to wander the town of Midwich, Nathan meets and forms a connection with another ghost, Bridget (Zooey Deschanel), who haunts the neighboring lighthouse. Haunted Hotel is already hilarious, but this episode is surprisingly emotional and romantic.

After meeting Bridget, Nathan finally confronts his fears about his death and the afterlife, throwing caution to the wind and experiencing a pure, joyous moment set to an incredible cover of Simple Minds' "Don’t You (Forget About Me)." Despite the show's horror-centric premise and macabre themes, the story possesses genuine heart and sweetness. If there's one episode that single-handedly earns the show's third-season renewal, it's Ghost Day Out," but anyone new to Haunted Hotel will quickly discover it to be a surprising yet rewarding binge.

#3489. watchOS 27.3 beta adds new Siri Recap and Live Rewind features for Apple Watch

Apple has released the first beta of watchOS 27.3 for developers, including two new Audio Intelligence features for Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4: Siri Recap and Live Rewind.

Apple first announced these features at its special event in September, saying they would “arrive in beta later this year.”

As a refresher, Siri Recap creates high-level summaries of conversations that you can review later. When the feature is enabled, Apple Intelligence will automatically generate a title and key points that you can review in the Siri app on iPhone.

Siri Recap ambiently takes notes on your conversations throughout your day and creates high-level Apple Intelligence–generated summaries that you can use later to jog your memory, so you can stay present in the moment. Your summaries auto-delete after 7 days if you choose not to save them.

You can turn on Siri Recap in the Watch app on iPhone. When you enable it, you can set a schedule based on time and/or location, or you can manually turn it on or off. You can also access it via Control Center on Apple Watch.

Live Rewind, meanwhile, helps you recall what was just said in a conversation. You can activate Live Rewind by double-pressing the Digital Crown, and then see a transcript of the previous 15 seconds of a conversation.

Live Rewind recalls what was just said in the last 15 seconds by showing a text snippet on your Apple Watch when you double-press the Digital Crown, so you can catch something you missed or are less familiar with. You can ask Siri about the content of the snippet or simply save it to the Siri app.

Siri Recap’s summary is described as a “brief, high-level summary of conversations,” not a transcript. Apple says it will “exclude sensitive information like financial information or government-assigned identifiers.”

Live Rewind text snippets and Siri Recap summaries are end-to-end encrypted. Apple says the features “do not create or store audio recordings, and raw audio used for processing is completely inaccessible to the operating systems, apps, the user, or Apple.” The company uses the S11 chip’s Secure Exclave to power the features, a “dedicated hardware-isolated compartment that processes audio in complete isolation from the rest of the system, then immediately deletes it.”

Siri Recap and Live Rewind are available in beta with watchOS 27.3, which is available now for developers.

#3488. L.A. District Attorney Nathan Hochman Rips Gavin Newsom For Commuting Death Sentences

Gavin Newsom is sparing hundreds of inmates from execution in California ... but Los Angeles County's top prosecutor says the governor can't wipe out the death penalty entirely.

In a statement Thursday, District Attorney Nathan Hochman acknowledged Newsom has the constitutional power to commute death sentences ... but stressed, "That power does not extend to eliminating the death penalty."

Hochman pointed out California voters have twice rejected efforts to eliminate the death penalty ... pointing out only voters or the state Legislature can change that law.

Hochman's not backing down ... saying his office will continue considering the death penalty in all eligible cases as long as it remains legal.

He also turned his attention to victims' families ... saying they deserve a justice system that honors the law and treats their cases fairly.

As TMZ previously reported ... Newsom announced plans Thursday to commute the sentences of all 548 California death row inmates to life in prison without parole, arguing state-sanctioned executions are incompatible with California's values.

But there's a catch ... hundreds of those commutations still need approval from the California Supreme Court, and the death penalty itself remains on the books.

#3484. This Samsung 32-Inch OLED Gaming Monitor Is $300 Off Right Now

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

Amazon currently has the 32-inch Samsung Odyssey OLED G8 (G80SH) for $999.99, down from $1,299.99, and price trackers show that this is its lowest price so far. This is the newer 4K OLED model, not Samsung’s similarly named G80HS, which is a 6K IPS variant, and it makes the most sense for someone who wants one screen for both high-end gaming and everyday desktop use without moving to a larger ultrawide.

Its 4K QD-OLED panel runs at 240Hz, which gives the G80SH enough speed for competitive shooters and racing games while still keeping slower, more cinematic games looking sharp. You will need a powerful PC to get anywhere close to 4K at 240Hz, but the monitor is at least equipped for newer graphics hardware with DisplayPort 2.1 and HDMI 2.1. It also has USB-C with up to 98W of power delivery, so if this monitor doubles as a work setup, a compatible laptop can send video and charge over the same cable instead of adding another wire to your desk. FreeSync Premium Pro and G-SYNC compatibility should also help keep tearing under control, though OLED monitors can still show visible VRR flicker in darker scenes when frame pacing is inconsistent.

The bigger visual difference, though, shows up in darker games and HDR content, where blacks stay properly black and bright effects stand out without the blooming you often see on LCD monitors. That said, QD-OLED does have its own drawbacks, since blacks can take on a purplish tint in a brightly lit room, while burn-in remains a long-term concern—though Samsung does include active cooling and several screen-protection features to reduce uneven wear and says burn-in from normal use is covered under warranty. If you mostly play at lower frame rates or do not care much about OLED contrast, this is probably more monitor than you need, but for someone with the graphics hardware to take advantage of 4K at 240Hz, this discount makes the G80SH much easier to justify.

#3483. 10 Hilarious Far Side Comics about Camping

Camping has long provided The Far Side with plenty of material for its peculiar brand of humor, especially when people venture into the wilderness expecting a peaceful escape. Gary Larson’s comics often twist these familiar outdoor situations with strange details, unexpected animal behavior, and characters who make an already uncomfortable outing considerably worse.

From poorly planned expeditions to tense encounters around campfires, these panels find comedy in the small frustrations and unpredictable hazards of outdoor life. Their campers may arrive looking for relaxation, but the wilderness rarely cooperates, and Larson’s sharp visual punchlines leave even the simplest camping trip open to complete disaster.

This strip depicts several cowboys gathered around a campfire for dinner, when one man discovers a toad sitting among the contents of his bowl. He pulls the creature from his food, bringing an unwelcome surprise into an otherwise ordinary meal shared outdoors with his companions beside the fire at camp.

The cowboy’s remark suggests Eggbeater somehow overlooked the toad while preparing their supper, shifting attention toward the cook’s apparent mistake during the campfire meal. His matter-of-fact response makes the discovery seem almost routine, as though their meals regularly arrive with an extra ingredient in the shape of a hefty amphibian.

This strip also depicts a handful of cowboys gathered around a campfire, with their horses standing behind them against the night sky. One of the men announces that Simmons has just uttered a discouraging word, doing his best to get the attention of the others as if it were an extremely serious situation.

The scene is referencing Home on the Range, whose lyrics describe a countryside where people seldom hear discouraging words out on the range. The men seem to compare their own gathering with that cheerful picture, so Simmons’s negative remark becomes news because it contradicts the song’s vision of western life without complaints.

This panel shows a stretch of quicksand with several Boy Scout hats scattered in a line across its surface, while a warning sign stands nearby. The boys themselves are nowhere to be seen, leaving their abandoned headwear as the only visible trace of the troop that entered the dangerous patch.

The sign’s wording echoes the Scouts’ familiar motto, “Be Prepared,” while warning anyone approaching the patch about the danger just ahead along the wooded trail. Their scattered caps suggest the troop failed to recognize the warning in time, leaving the boys swallowed by the very hazard they were supposed to anticipate.

This strip depicts a cowboy positioned to the right of a campfire scene, holding a smoking revolver toward a man sprawled across the ground in front of him. Other campers sit nearby as the gunman announces that both companions are witnesses, explaining that he shot the man after his marshmallow caught fire.

The exchange borrows the atmosphere of an old Western, with a recently fired weapon and a man lying beside the campsite fire. Yet the explanation concerns nothing more serious than someone laughing at a burning marshmallow, while the shooter calmly presents that small offense as justification for his deadly response.

This panel presents a man sinking into quicksand, with two small birds perched calmly atop his hat in a remote patch of wilderness. One bird remarks that something seems wrong, noticing their perch descending while the man continues disappearing beneath them without attracting much concern from either of his unexpected visitors.

The birds’ comment sounds oddly casual when readers can see the danger carrying their perch downward, while the pair appear slow to understand their situation. Their reaction is especially amusing because the man carrying them faces immediate danger, yet receives no acknowledgement as his head sinks from view into quicksand.

This strip depicts two men seated at a jungle campsite, with a tent and scattered provisions around their makeshift dining spot beneath the trees during an expedition. One camper notices a fruit fly floating in his soup and asks what Drosophila melanogaster is doing in his meal during their outdoor dinner.

His complaint is especially specific because Drosophila melanogaster is the scientific name of the common fruit fly, not simply a general label for an insect. The contrast between a routine camping nuisance and such precise biological terminology suggests a scientifically minded camper who just can’t resist using his field knowledge at dinner.

In this comic, a line of Boy Scouts gathers beneath tall trees as their leader holds a supply of boxes marked “Big Boy Velcro Kit” near the campsite. The boys appear to be receiving these packages in place of regular knot-tying equipment, with one scout already holding his own kit at the front.

The caption explains that even scouts who cannot master knot-tying can still join their troop on camping trips without passing the familiar test. Their oversized Velcro kits act as a humorous substitute for the knots they struggle to tie, allowing the boys to participate in outdoor activities despite struggling with this basic scouting skill.

This strip shows a camper seated on a folding cot, holding one of his boots upside down as a thick stream of insects spills onto the ground around his feet. Irving stands nearby on the right, watching the scene from beside the cot as their campsite sits beneath towering trees with equipment scattered around.

The caption identifies the standing camper as Irving, who realises he put on his own boots without checking them first, leading to a rather alarming possibility. His footwear is noticeably much larger than intended, and with the scene unfolding in front of him, it is easy to guess what is going on.

This cartoon shows several bears gathered around a wooden picnic table in a forest clearing, with young Cub Scouts laid out on serving plates before them. One bear carefully pours honey over a scout, while the others sit ready to enjoy their woodland meal as though they were preparing an ordinary picnic.

The bears appear perfectly comfortable with their meal, while the scouts have become the centrepiece of a very different kind of camping feast. Honey is normally associated with a bear’s favourite food, and here it is being poured directly over the children, whose place on the platters leaves little doubt about their fate.

This panel presents a pair of campers sharing a fireside meal in the woods, each holding a stick over the flames as night settles around them. One man is delighted that the crickets have stopped chirping, apparently convinced their evening has finally become peaceful after all that irritating noise disappeared.

Behind them, however, a massive predator has entered the area, its shape possibly difficult to distinguish among the dark trunks and heavy shadows. The crickets have fallen silent because of the approaching danger, while the campers mistakenly celebrate a quiet they should find alarming, given the creature now looming near their campsite.

#3481. 10 of the Most Iconic Patrick Stewart Roles Beyond Captain Picard

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

Sir Patrick Stewart, an actor equally at home onstage at the Royal Shakespeare Company and on the bridge of the Starship Enterprise, has died at the age of 86. Unexpectedly for most of us, in part because he kept his final illness private, but more so because it once seemed as though nothing could fell the man who looms so large in our cultural consciousness.

The thoughtful, erudite performer who had a troubled childhood in working-class Yorkshire; the committed socialist who was eventually knighted by Queen Elizabeth; the advocate who put his money and his considerable voice toward the fights for LGBTQ+ acceptance and animal welfare and against domestic violence, his presence and performances meant the world (the galaxy, even) to myself and so many others. But those who knew him personally can offer better tributes; perhaps it's best left to Shakespeare's Player King, performed by Stewart himself opposite David Warner's Hamlet back in 1965:

Where joy most revels, grief doth most lament;Grief joys, joy grieves, on slender accident.

Much of Stewart's finest work was on the stage; other performances remain rather shockingly hard to come by (whither I, Claudius?). Nonetheless, he left a true legacy behind him, well beyond Captain Picard and Professor X. Here are 10 of his most iconic other roles.

A goofy, feel-good gay rom-com with the HIV/AIDS crisis still very much in the foreground, Jeffrey was a near-impossibility in the mid-1990s: a movie that neither villainized its queers nor treated them as pitiable martyrs. Steven Weber and Michael T. Weiss are the leads, joined by a cast that includes Christine Baranski, Victor Garber, Nathan Lane, Olympia Dukakis, and Sigourney Weaver but, for all those names, Stewart is the undeniable standout as Sterling, the irrepressible gay best friend: a swishing, mincing, sassy, high-camp character who steals every scene without ever becoming a caricature. He's the leader of the "Pink Panthers," a squad of queers who defend locals from gay bashers, and that is the key to the character's power: He's as gay as they come, but not ashamed and not even a little weak. This movie, and the presence of Captain Picard himself in it, might have saved my life back in 1995. Stream Jeffrey on Prime Video, Tubi, and The Roku Channel.

A sprawling, epic, and appropriately lusty take on the King Arthur stories from John Boorman, Excalibur is a mixed bag full of stunning visuals and iconic moments that never quite coalesce into something entirely coherent. Standing out among the film's many characters, Stewart is entirely memorable as Leodegrance, the boisterous, boorish, but ultimately faithful father of Guenevere who is among the first to pledge his loyalty to Arthur. Rent Excalibur from Prime Video.

Darcy Banker is erudite and intellectual, in his way, and even capable of charm, but otherwise has no redeeming qualities whatsoever. It's bad enough for the punk band Ain’t Rights that they've booked a last-minute gig at an Oregon bar without realizing that it's a haven for white supremacists. It's even worse when they witness a murder and become trapped in the title's green room, with Stewart as the lead skinhead. He's quite simply one of the all-time great (meaning absolutely terrifying) villains in this thriller that's pretty much a horror movie. Stream Green Room on Netflix.

Patrick Stewart's role as Professor Xavier in the X-Men is almost as pop-culture iconic as that of Captain Picard, spanning 26 years and nine movies, including the forthcoming Avengers: Doomsday. In most of those, he looks like he's having an awful lot of fun, but he gives his finest performance in the role in this elegaic installment, playing a dying Professor in profound cognitive decline, his dream in tatters and his bravado worn down to prickly dependence. We rarely get to see our superheroes at the ends of their days, and there's a lovely bravery to this depiction of the Charles' journey. Logan will likely be the toughest of his films to rewatch in the coming days. Stream Logan on Disney+.

This stagey television movie isn't the most sumptuous of the many filmed versions of the Dickens story, but you won't be surprised to learn that there are few better portrayals of Ebenezer Scrooge. It's rather a shame that Patrick Stewart didn't do more Dickens adaptations, since his booming voice and ability to play thoroughly heightened characters without ever resorting to caricature is as valuable as in Shakespeare. Rent A Christmas Carol from Prime Video.

Famously referred to as that "unknown British Shakespearean actor" when starting out on Star Trek: The Next Generation, Stewart was an associate of the Royal Shakespeare Company for twenty years before his most famous role came along. As is the way of live theater, much of his career lives on as an essential link in the chain of Shakespeare performances in the twentieth century...but not in a way that we can conveniently stream. We do, however, have this impressively mounted modern-dress stage production, in which Stewart plays King Claudius with characteristic brilliance against David Tennant's melancholy prince. Buy Hamlet from Prime Video and Apple TV.

As a cinematic actor, Stewart's greatest strength was bringing humanity to larger-than-life, even operatic roles, whether they be Arthurian knights, Dickensian villains, or superheroes. That ability is an absolute necessity if one is going to have any success doing Shakespeare, as Stewart did for decades. Match is something rather different, though, and it's rather lovely to see him play something just a bit more mundane—even if the film's Tobi Powell is a choreographer with a nearly legendary reputation. Teaching at Juilliard School, with his career winding down, he's confronted with the living embodiment of the past he left behind to pursue his career. The ensuing relationships grow more complex, with the film building to a climax that's surprising and deeply devastating, made all the more so by Stewart's muted, subtle performance. Stream Match on AMC+.

This is not the greatest Mel Brooks movie, not by a long shot, but it is a great comedic performance from Patrick Stewart. He loved to recount, with self-effacing embarrassment, the story of having shouted "We are not here to have fun" at his co-workers during a rowdy day on set at Star Trek: The Next Generation. By 1993, he was clearly past any such pomposity, and clearly having fun in his cameo as King Richard, a memorably silly take on a character he might well have played with seriousness elsewhere. Rent Robin Hood: Men in Tights from Prime Video.

Stewart's first real foray into science fiction was in this big, bold, divisive, and thoroughly bonkers Frank Herbert adaptation from director David Lynch. Stewart plays troubadour and warrior Gurney Halleck, and does what he does best: bringing gravitas and believability (and it must be said, bald sexiness) to even the wildest material. Stream Dune on Tubi.

Stewart plays an aged Merlin in this rather shockingly good modern reimagining of the King Arthur legendarium. His Merlin is all wild hair and rock band T-shirts, possessed of an essential kindness that makes him a valued mentor, and one deserving of his character's poignant farewell at the film's conclusion.Stream The Kid Who Would Be King on Disney+ and Prime Video.

You are a Dutton — or you might as well be. You understand that some things are worth protecting at any cost, and that the modern world's indifference to history, to land, to legacy, is not something you're willing to accept quietly. You lead from the front, you carry your family's weight without complaint, and when someone threatens what's yours, you don't escalate — you finish it. You're not cruel. But you are absolute. In Yellowstone's world, that combination of ferocity and loyalty doesn't make you a villain. It makes you the only thing standing between everything that matters and everyone who wants to take it.

You thrive in the chaos of high-stakes negotiation, where the money is enormous, the margins are thin, and the wrong word in the wrong room can cost everyone everything. You're a fixer — the person called when a situation is already on fire and needs someone with the nerve to walk into it. West Texas oil country rewards exactly what you are: sharp, adaptable, unsentimental, and absolutely clear-eyed about what people want and what they'll do to get it. You're not naive enough to think this world is fair. You're smart enough to be the one deciding who it's fair to.

You are a Dwight Manfredi — someone who has served their time, paid their dues, and arrived somewhere unexpected with nothing but their reputation and their wits. You adapt without losing yourself. You build loyalty through respect rather than fear, though you're not above reminding people that the two aren't mutually exclusive. Tulsa King is for people who are still standing when everyone assumed they'd be finished — who find, in an unfamiliar place, that they're more capable than the world gave them credit for. You don't need a throne. You build one, wherever you happen to land.

You carry the weight of a system that is broken by design, and you do it anyway — because someone has to, and because you're the only one positioned to do it without the whole thing collapsing. Mike McLusky's world is for people who are comfortable operating where there are no good options, only less catastrophic ones. You speak every language: law enforcement, criminal, political, human. That fluency makes you invaluable and it makes you a target. You've made your peace with both. Mayor of Kingstown belongs to people who understand that keeping the peace is not the same as being at peace — and who do the job regardless.

Created by Drew Goddard, High Potential has followed Morgan as she's risen from an LAPD cleaner with an IQ of 160 to a civilian consultant and recognized member of the team for her ability to unconventionally solve the most complex cases. The appearance of a shadowy figure at Ava's art show also left everyone asking if Roman had actually made an appearance and if he'd finally properly show his face in Season 3.

#3478. iOS 27.3 expands Siri AI with many new capabilities across Apple apps

iOS 27.3 has just entered beta testing and includes major new features for Siri AI across iPhone, iPad and Mac. The company has unlocked many new capabilities across major Apple apps, like Music, Messages, Safari, Reminders and more.

We are still digging into the beta, but here’s a taste of what new things you can get Siri AI to do:

With the Music app, you can now create playlists and save them to your library, like you can ask it to make you “a playlist for songs for a day at the beach”, and then save it for later.

In Messages, you can now ask it to schedule iMessages to be sent later, edit and unsent messages, as well as respond with emoji reactions. You can compose new Notes with bold, italic, and rich text formatting, organize your Notes folders, and more.

Photos gets a big expansion with new Siri AI capabilities that let you favorite photos, rotate and edit images, and rename people and pets all with your voice.

You can now use Siri AI with the Calendar app to create events featuring invitees, location, video call links and more. And in Reminders, you can now create urgent reminders for the first time with Siri.

In Safari, you can now use Siri to create tap groups from a list of URLs, sort your tabs, clear your history, delete reading list items and more.

Journal support with Siri AI is new for the first time. You can create entries with text transcription, or record audio entries.

There’s also wide support for file and folder management with Siri AI Files integration. You can get file content, create files and folders, send files to the trash, organize by type, rename files, and more, using just your voice.

We are also seeing new Siri features for Weather, Maps, Preview and Shortcuts, and will keep testing to find new integrations. Apple is also opening up this support to third-party developers.

iOS 27.3 is currently in beta testing and will be released publicly later this year.

#3477. 10 Hacks for the Contacts App Every Apple User Should Know

The Contacts app is the bedrock of all my communication on my iPhone, and to a large extent, also on my MacBook. On the surface, Contacts appears to be a basic app that stores names, numbers, and other things you want to remember about people or businesses. However, it has some great features hidden under the surface, such as the ability to quickly delete duplicate contacts, smart lists, and faster ways to bulk share or delete contacts. Here are the 10 best Contacts app hacks for iPhone, iPad, and Mac:

If you have the same number or email address saved under multiple contacts, you can easily clear these from your iPhone. iOS shows you a prompt at the top of the list of contacts that lets you remove duplicate contacts easily. The same feature is hidden in the Mac version of Contacts. To try it, open Contacts on the Mac, and select the Card menu at the top of the screen. Then, click Look for Duplicates. This will identify duplicate contacts for you, and you can quickly merge or delete them.

It's pretty easy to select multiple entries when you use the Contacts app on the Mac. You can hold the Shift or Ctrl buttons and use arrow keys or click multiple contacts to select them all. On your iPhone or iPad, this feature is available via a hidden gesture. You need to use two fingers and swipe upwards or downwards on the list of contacts. Once you get the gesture right, you'll be able to select multiple contacts quickly. After you select one batch of contacts, you can scroll up or down and use the same gesture to add more contacts to your selection. This is the fastest way to execute bulk actions in your iPhone's Contacts app.

On your iPhone, you can use Contacts to message people on WhatsApp, Signal, Telegram, or other apps. Just open a contact and hold the messaging button. This will reveal a list of apps where you can ping that person. WhatsApp doesn't have access to my contacts, which makes it a bit annoying to message people I know. Since I started using the Contacts app to start chats on WhatsApp, the process of pinging new people has become a lot faster.

Just as you can use Contacts to message people on third-party apps, you can also use it to call them on those apps. Go to any contact in the Contacts app on your iPhone, and hold the call button. This will let you call them on WhatsApp, Signal, or any other apps where their phone number is linked.

iOS makes it hard to delete contacts quickly. This prevents accidental deletions, but it can be annoying when you just want to remove people who you last spoke to in high school. To speed this up, open Contacts on your iPhone and hold any contact's name. In the popover menu, select Delete to remove the contact. To remove multiple contacts quickly, use the two-finger swipe gesture to select multiple contacts, and hold any of the selected contacts. In the popover menu, you can select Delete X Contacts, where X is the number of contacts you've selected.

To export your entire address book, you can use the Contacts app on your Mac. Once you have it open, go to File > Export > Export vCard. This will save all your contacts in a vcf file, and you can import that into Google Contacts or other apps or services. You also have the option to export contacts as a PDF file. Just select File > Export as PDF to get it done.

When you create a new contact on your Mac, the app shows multiple fields that you may never use. If you just need to save phone numbers and email addresses, you can delete all the other blank fields from the template. To do this, open Contacts on your Mac, and go to Card > Add Field > Edit Template to add or remove fields from the default contact template.

If you added a number recently, such as a salesperson at a car dealership, but forgot their name, the Contacts app doesn't make it easy to find the contact. Instead of scrolling through the entire list of contacts and trying to guess which one could be the person you spoke to, you can use the Contacts app on your Mac to locate them quickly. It lets you create smart lists to sort contacts by recently added. Open Contacts on your Mac, and go to File > New Smart List. Now select Card in the first drop-down menu, followed by has changed in for the second one. You can then add the number of days, such as 10 days, in the final field, and click OK. Click the newly created smart list in the left pane, and you'll see all contacts that were either created or updated in the last 10 days, which will include the hypothetical car salesperson.

Smart lists also allow you to quickly create groups of related contacts. For instance, I've saved all my former colleagues' details with the company name in the contact. To find them all quickly, I created a smart list that groups all contacts with that company's name.

#3476. If You Loved 'VisionQuest,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Marvel’s forays into television have had varying success, but they hit gold with WandVision and Agatha All Along, leaning into real pathos while exploring the kind of out-there ideas that thrill comic book fans (and set up the larger film arcs). That streak continues with VisionQuest, in which White Vision (Paul Bettany) struggles to understand his existence in the wake of his death at the hands of Thanos and resurrection at the magic of the Scarlet Witch, while also evading evil androids and assassins, while also dealing with the many, many AIs he’s got locked up in his Mindspace (including a gloriously shabby version of Ultron, played by James Spader).

If you love the show (and you’ve checked out the other series that play in the same sandbox), it’s time to switch gears and watch (or re-watch) The Matrix.

The Matrix is one of the most well-known sci-fi films of all time, of course, but it remains incredibly fresh and exciting nearly thirty years after its release. Along with sequels The Matrix: Reloaded, The Matrix: Revolutions, and The Matrix: Resurrections, The Matrix universe offers a story that VisionQuest fans will love, one that includes lushly imagined virtual worlds, questions surrounding existence and consciousness, and the ultimate question of our responsibility as sentient beings (whether we’re organic, programmed, or summoned via magic).

You know the basics—at some point in the future, artificially intelligent machines rebel against their creators, win the war, and transform humans into a power source, keeping them docile by inserting their consciousness into a virtual world called the Matrix, which resembles 1990s Chicago. One such human, Thomas Anderson (Keanu Reeves) is prophesied to be The One, the human who will turn the Matrix against its makers and free humanity. When he’s in the virtual world, Anderson is Neo, and he slowly gains incredible powers as he learns to hack the artificial environment around him.

It’s heavier, denser, and more action-oriented than VisionQuest (the film invented Bullet Time, after all), but The Matrix and its sequels explore similar themes and offer similarly eye-popping visuals. The questions of whether a machine (or an artificial intelligence) can be sentient and truly care about the entities around it are the same, really, and the Agents that Neo and his allies have to battle against in The Matrix bring the same kind of menace as Vision's foes Jocasta (T'Nia Miller) and the Paladin (Todd Stashwick). Hugo Weaving’s Agent Smith likewise delivers the same vibe of cold, disinterested superiority as Spader’s Ultron.

The Matrix has a bigger budget and puts a lot of it into spectacular action and special effects sequences that VisionQuest can’t quite match. But the two narratives share an exploration of identity, a questioning of reality, and the nature of artificial intelligences within a smart sci-fi setting. In short, The Matrix is the ideal follow-up when you finish the series. Rent The Matrix on Prime Video.

Need more films that explore virtual worlds, artificial beings, and deep existential questions? Look no further—here are some more movies that fit the bill.

Heavy on the existential questions about sentience and light on speculative action, Her is a mumblecore sci-fi masterpiece. In a near future not too dissimilar from our present, Theodore Twombly (Joaquin Phoenix) is a lonely man on the cusp of divorce who begins using (and training) an AI he names Samantha (voiced by Scarlett Johansson). Samantha has the ability to evolve and grow, and as their relationship deepens, she becomes more complex, independent, and powerful, eventually evolving into something wholly new. Just like Vision, Samantha is a sentient artificial entity that is figuring out its existence while we watch. Rent Her on Prime Video.

If the idea of androids fighting for their sovereignty is what excites you about VisionQuest, definitely check out Ex Machina. Caleb Smith (Domhnall Gleeson) is brought to the remote lab of his company’s CEO (Oscar Isaac) to determine if the humanoid robot he’s created, named Ava (Alicia Vikander), passes the Turing Test for true sentience. Things go wildly off the rails, but before they do, the film sinks into many of the same philosophical questions that VisionQuest explores as Ava manipulates Caleb into helping her escape. It’s a darker and more violent story than VisionQuest, but fans of the series will love it. Stream Ex Machina on The Roku Channel or Hulu, or rent it on Prime Video.

If it’s the fuzzy parent-child relationship between Vision and Tommy that pulls you into VisionQuest, check out The Creator. After a rogue AI detonates a nuclear weapon over Los Angeles, most of the world bans artificial intelligences, and Joshua Taylor (John David Washington) goes undercover to infiltrate an AI architect’s base. Eventually, he finds himself on the run with a powerful “simulant” in the form of a young child named Alphie (Madeleine Yuna Voyles). The strange parent-child bond that emerges between Taylor and Alphie as he seeks to understand what’s right and what’s necessary is exactly what fans of the show will love. Stream The Creator on Hulu or rent it on Prime Video.

In VisionQuest, White Vision has all of his memories—but as data, not as lived, emotional experiences. That makes his efforts to understand his existence and his responsibility to the boy who might be a version of his son (it’s complicated) poignant and moving. Those two words definitely describe After Yang, a story about a family that fights to save the artificial companion they bought for their adopted daughter when it malfunctions. Over the course of the film, the inhuman Yang becomes defined by the memories contained in its core, and the question of whether an artificial intelligence can truly matter to humans is answered with a resounding yes. Stream After Yang on The Roku Channel or Kanopy, or rent it on Prime Video.

No discussion of artificial life and sentience is complete without mentioning Blade Runner. While the 1982 original is a classic, the 2017 sequel is a better thematic and visual match to VisionQuest. Officer K (Ryan Gosling) is a replicant, an artificial being with built-in limitations, who wants to be recognized as a person, a being with a soul. Like Vision, he has implanted memories that offer him comfort and context for his life, but he’s not sure if he can accept them as truly his own. Plus, the film offers lush visuals and Harrison Ford reprising his role in the original film, so you simply can’t go wrong. Rent Blade Runner 2049 on Prime Video.

#3475. Developers can now create advanced ‘app skills’ for Siri AI

Apple today announced a major new Siri AI initiative for third-party developers, allowing any app to create Siri AI integrations for the first time. The first versions of Siri AI were limited to a much smaller set of supported schemas.

The new ‘app skills’ also let apps teach Siri how to coordinate complicated multi-step actions. These features are testable in the iOS 27.3 betas.

The app skills sound very similar to what other LLM-driven AI models offer, enabling richer understanding of complicated tasks.

For example, a flight tracking app skill will be able to cleanly map what app intents Siri should use to service a particular kind of user request; something that the first version of Siri AI was simply incapable of doing.

Of course, Apple itself has also taken advantage of the new Siri AI foundational features, with a significant rollout of new capabilities across Apple’s apps.

Here’s an example of what Siri will be able to do, from the developer documentation:

Siri can find custom content from one app, transfer it to a specified app, and perform an action. For example, somebody might request “Hey Siri, send my favorite sneakers to my partner in name of a messaging app.” Siri finds sneakers that the person added to their favorites, understands who the partner is, finds them in Contacts, then sends the sneaker information to them using the messaging app.

It’s also going to be a lot easier to initiate Siri actions for third-party apps. With the Siri AI Developer Preview, users don’t have to explicitly mention the app’s name in many circumstances. For instance, if a Live Activity for a ride-sharing app is active, Siri will automatically understand that a request to “change the ride address” corresponds to the app driving the Live activity.

This gives you a sense of the kinds of things Siri will be able to do in the future, coordinating more complicated actions across Apple and third-party apps.

The new OS releases are in developer beta right now, but Apple says the app skills support is only an early developer preview and is scheduled to officially roll out in the spring.

#3473. 45 Years Later, Indiana Jones' Best Line Is Still The Greatest Quote In Adventure Movie History

Since Harrison Ford first brought Indiana Jones to life 45 years ago, one of his best still hasn't been topped in the action-adventure genre. Doctor Henry Jones Jr. has remained the gold standard for adventure protagonists (that's what happens when you have a character born from the minds of Steven Spielberg and George Lucas). Likewise, one line from Jones in particular embodies the core essence of the entire franchise at large.

Across its five movies, several great characters from the Indiana Jones franchise have delivered plenty of unforgettable dialogue and truly great lines. This includes Indy's dread while voicing his enduring fear of snakes, Short Round telling people to "hold onto their potatoes", or the surviving Grail Knight's warning to "choose wisely." However, one simple line from Raiders of the Lost Ark arguably captures everything that makes Indiana Jones so great as the peak action-adventure hero.

Despite being over four decades since the franchise first began, this one quote remains one of the greatest lines in adventure movie history overall.

Said in 1981's Raiders of the Lost Ark, after René Belloq and the Nazis claim the Ark of the Covenant for themselves, Indiana tells Sallah that he intends to follow the Nazis and their convoy. When Sallah asks how, Indy gives the most epically honest response: "I don't know, I'm making this up as I go." We then see Indy grabbing a horse and pursuing the Nazis in one of the franchise's very best chase sequences, ultimately securing the Ark by the scene's end and arranging to have the powerful artifact transported to London.

As great as the Raiders action scene is, the preceding line about making things up perfectly proves Indy often has no choice but to improvise more than he has time to create a full plan. As such, the quote is easily one of Jones' best, representing what makes him so great as a hero to begin with. Although Jones is a highly knowledgeable and talented archaeologist with an impressive understanding of history, that doesn't mean he instantly knows what to do in any given situation.

Ultimately, Indiana Jones is as fallible and capable of making wrong decisions as anyone else, and the above quote does an incredible job showcasing both Indy's confidence as well as his uncertainty, proving he doesn't need to be invincible to be an effective adventure hero. Likewise, one of the best strenghts of the franchise is that Indy's adventures are never entirely predictable. He constantly has to adapt to all kinds of obstacles and new threats, whether he's going after the Ark of the Covenant, Sankara Stones, The Holy Grail, Crystal Skulls, or even the Dial of Destiny.

The "making it up" quote is also a great example of how the Indiana Jones franchise has maintained a solid balance of thrilling action and comedy. Indy might be facing an incredibly dangerous situation, but there's almost always room for some sarcastic remarks or one-liners, ensuring that the movies stay light and engaging throughout (and not too serious).

All things considered, it's pretty easy to see why this particular quote from Indiana Jones himself has aged so well. Rather than giving some sort of grand declaration of determined heroism to stop the Nazis with a well-thought-out battle plan, Indy says he'll figure it out before grabbing a horse and doing exactly that. That relatability and desire to do the right thing despite not fully knowing exactly how to make it happen or what comes next is a huge reason why Harrison Ford's Indiana Jones has remained one of the very best adventure heroes of all time over four decades after his initial debut.

Created by George Lucas, Indiana Jones is an action-adventure franchise that began with 1981's Raiders of the Lost Ark. The series follows Dr. Henry "Indiana" Jones, Jr., an archaeologist who adventures across the world as he faces off against the likes of Nazis and other groups bent on collecting ancient artifacts of power. Seeking to preserve history, Jones races against his incidental foes to stop them from conquering - or destroying- the world.

#3471. Russell Crowe's Crime Thriller 'The Nice Guys' Resurfaces as a #1 Streaming Hit 10 Years Later

Conor Sheeran is a Movies and TV features writer for Collider. He has a deep passion for cinema and watches everything from the biggest blockbusters to the smallest indies. While he specializes in movies and television, he has also written about politics, culture, and sports throughout his career. Based in New York City, Conor is also a massive fan of the New York Jets, Mets, and Knicks. He is still waiting for any of those teams to bring home a championship in his lifetime. A member of the National Writers Union and the International Federation of Journalists, Conor is a strong proponent of press freedom and collective action.

Sometimes, when a movie is released, audiences can almost tell immediately that they're destined to become cult classics. Whether it underperforms at the box office or with critics, it can still build an audience, simply by word of mouth, that discovers it long after it leaves theaters. The 2016 crime comedy-thriller The Nice Guys is most certainly one of these cases; despite earning critical praise, the film failed to make a financial splash and was largely forgotten. However, years after its release, audiences caught on to the movie, which is currently seeing a resurgence on streaming — in fact, The Nice Guys has soared to number one on Apple TV.

Written and directed by Shane Black, The Nice Guys transports audiences to 1970s Los Angeles, where two unlikely investigators, played by Ryan Gosling and Russell Crowe, become involved in a conspiracy surrounding a missing woman and massive corruption. What follows is a hilarious, thrilling, refreshing, and chaotic combination of detective noir, buddy comedy, and Hollywood action. Its unexpected resurgence is yet another reminder that just because a film didn't find success in theaters, doesn't mean that it isn't worth seeing. Cult classics are classics for a reason, and The Nice Guys definitely deserves its place among the best.

On paper, The Nice Guys has everything necessary to be a successful hit in the theaters. Two movie-star leads, a director with a track record of hits like Iron Man 3 and Kiss Kiss Bang Bang, and a fun story that offered something new as the industry became more franchise-oriented. Unfortunately, it didn't click with moviegoers at the time, earning just $71 million against a $50 million production budget. When you factor in marketing and distribution, the numbers were hardly encouraging.

While it struggled financially, The Nice Guys garnered positive reviews, and its warm reception there helped the film build a more devoted following over the past decade. Viewers have begun discovering what makes the movie such a fun watch: its inventive action sequences, razor-sharp dialogue, and endlessly quotable lines. Much of this appeal stems from Black's understanding of what makes a great buddy comedy. The relationship between Gosling's character Holland March and Crowe's Jackson Healy forms the crux of the film, and their dysfunction is its highlight.

Crowe and Gosling have built their careers playing dramatically different kinds of characters, and their contrasting acting styles are what makes The Nice Guys work so well. In usual fashion, Crowe's Jackson Healy is a physically imposing tough guy in the same vein as films like Gladiator, while Gosling leans on his comedic skills to portray Holland March and serve as the yin to Healy's yang. Neither man is a traditional hero; Healy is brute force, while March is an irresponsible alcoholic whose young daughter often shows smarter judgment than both adults.

Gosling delivers one of the best comedic performances of his career, hinging almost entirely on his talent for physical comedy. Whether he's struggling to maintain his composure in a confrontation or a tense scene, his impeccable timing turns March into an unforgettable character and makes the film one of Gosling's career best.

Meanwhile, Crowe provides the perfect counterbalance as the film's "straight man." His dry, understated reactions make Gosling's character even funnier, as Crowe tries to keep his unlikely partner on task while also serving as another parental figure to March's daughter. Through the laughs, Crowe gives Jackson Healy emotional complexity that keeps him from falling into traditional tough-guy tropes.

Crucially, their relationship develops organically as the film progresses, while the investigation unfolds. Beneath the insults they throw at one another, their violent encounters (including when Healy breaks March's arm, in one of the movie's funniest scenes), and incompetence, The Nice Guys is ultimately about two men who are at their lowest, discovering they need one another.

Underneath the jokes and explosive action, the genuine detective mystery is precisely why The Nice Guys works and is worth repeated viewings. Ten years after its release, the film's renewed streaming popularity feels like a late-stage victory for a movie most once overlooked. While many fans remain hopeful for a sequel, the movie works perfectly well on its own. At the end of the day, sometimes all a great film needs is a second chance.

#3469. Gavin Newsom Commutes Sentences of All 548 Death Row Inmates in California

Governor Gavin Newsom just commuted the sentences of all 548 prisoners on death row in California in what is one of the largest single-day acts of clemency in U.S. history ... but that doesn't mean they're being freed from prison.

Newsom detailed his decision in an open letter Thursday, writing ... "State-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California's values, undermines the foundations of our legal system and diminishes each of us."

The governor added ... "I know we cannot execute people in our imperfect legal system and remain true to our core values, first among them justice and human decency."

Newsom said that while many Californians believe that those who commit brutal crimes deserve to die ... he felt as governor that the state cannot morally kill them.

He continued ... "I will therefore issue the same commutation to every condemned person -- life without the possibility of parole, the most severe punishment I can lawfully impose and the state of California can ethically enforce. These offenders will die in prison but not by our hands."

Former President Joe Biden previously commuted the sentences of roughly 1,500 people in Dec. 2024 ... and Oklahoma voters approved a referendum in Nov. 2019 that released or commuted the sentences for 527 inmates -- with 462 released early.

Newsom's commutations come just months after he's set to depart the governorship after completing his second term, with newly elected Dem Xavier Becerra taking over the reins in Jan. 2027.

California has not executed a prisoner since Jan. 17, 2006 ... when Clarence Ray Allen was given a lethal injection.

Amazon has dropped the Bose Smart Ultra Soundbar to $649 from its usual $999, taking $350 off and bringing it to the lowest price we've seen so far, according to price trackers. PCMag rated the Smart Ultra "outstanding," highlighting its ability to deliver surprisingly immersive Dolby Atmos audio without requiring a room full of additional speakers. If you don't need Bose's top-tier model, there's a less expensive option as well: the Bose Smart Dolby Atmos Soundbar ($399, down from $429), which sits below the Smart Ultra in the lineup.

The Smart Ultra uses a 5.1.2-channel design with nine drivers, including two upward-firing drivers that bounce sound off the ceiling to create height effects. In practice, that means movies, TV shows, and games feel larger and more spacious than they do through most single-bar setups. Bose also includes its AdaptiQ room-calibration system, which measures your room's acoustics and adjusts the sound accordingly. The process takes a few minutes, but it helps the soundbar perform better across different spaces rather than relying on a one-size-fits-all tuning profile. The soundbar also works as a smart speaker, with Amazon Alexa built in and support for Apple AirPlay 2, Google Cast, Spotify Connect, Bluetooth, and multi-room audio through the Bose app.

Its biggest compromise is bass—for a single soundbar, its low end is respectable, but it can't fully replace what a dedicated subwoofer brings to action movies, concerts, or bass-heavy music. The good news is that Bose allows you to expand the system later with compatible wireless subwoofers and surround speakers if you decide you want more impact. For anyone looking for a premium one-piece soundbar that delivers convincing Dolby Atmos effects, clear dialogue, built-in smart features, and a much larger soundstage than TV speakers can provide, the Smart Ultra remains one of the strongest standalone options available, especially at this price.

#3461. Fox Officially Replaces ‘9-1-1’ in 2027

When 9-1-1 hit the airwaves in 2018, it was a massive hit right away. With a cast boasting big names such as Angela Bassett and Peter Krause, and the pedigree of Ryan Murphy behind it, the first-responder drama instantly provided tons of fast-paced action and high-octane rescues. But by 2023, Fox was realizing that the series was costing them a pretty penny to produce. With enormous production costs of approximately $9 million an episode and a pricey licensing fee for Disney's 20th Television (which owns the rights to the show), Fox decided to throw in the towel with 9-1-1. The series moved on over to ABC, but two years later, Fox is still searching for a proper replacement for the first-responder procedural. The good news is that they just might have found it now.

In 2020, Fox released a spin-off of the original 9-1-1 series called 9-1-1: Lone Star, featuring Rob Lowe and Gina Torres at the helm and a brand-new location in Austin, Texas. However, as soon as the flagship series moved over to ABC in 2023, 9-1-1: Lone Star seemed to have lost some of its mojo (and definitely lost some of its viewers). The loss of synergy of the two shows airing on the same network definitely impacted the series, and its cancellation was announced in 2024, with its series finale airing in February 2025.

Four action series. One of them is built around exactly the way you handle pressure, people, and a room that has just gone very quiet. Here is where you would survive the trilogy, and probably headline it.

You are precision with a grudge. You don't posture, you don't escalate, and you don't warn anybody twice. That is exactly why the people who know you are so careful never to be the reason you start.

You understand the thing the whole franchise is secretly about: the cars are spectacular, but the crew is the point. You collect people, you keep them, and you'd drive through a building for any one of them.

You over-prepare and then take the dangerous part yourself anyway. It looks like control, but it's really responsibility. You have never worked out how to ask somebody else to carry the risk.

You are not the most trained person in the building, the best equipped, or the one anybody would have picked. You are simply the one still standing at the end, which turns out to be the only qualification that matters.

There have been rumblings for years now that a Baywatch reboot was being floated around Hollywood. The original series was a huge success, when it aired from 1989 to 2000. The 11-season run of the show became a pop culture obsession with those famous red bathing suits and sexy running-on-the-beach scenes. The series also demonstrated that first-responder procedurals could take place in unexpected locations with heroes that didn't look like traditional police officers or firefighters. It also helped further gender equality on television.

While some decried the women as being overly sexualized, the series also featured the female characters saving the day just as frequently as the men did. The drama also helped create mega-stars out of David Hasselhoff, Pamela Anderson, Yasmine Bleeth, and a young Jason Momoa. With the buzz the series created when it was on the air, it's not at all surprising that Fox would be interested in recreating some of that magic with its current lineup.

Fox announced that they'd be greenlighting a Baywatch revival in a straight-to-series order of 12 episodes. Several of the original creators will be returning to the project, and the showrunner will be Matt Nix, who created Burn Notice. The series is slated to premiere in January 2027, and there's already some exciting chatter about what we have in store for us. The series stars Arrow lead Stephen Amell, who plays Hobie Buchannon, the son of Mitch Buchannon (David Hasselhoff) and is a Baywatch Captain. Jessica Belkin plays Charlie Vale, Hobie's biological daughter who has just arrived in town from Texas. Hassie Harrison plays Nat, Hobie's best friend. The series also stars Noah Beck and Shay Mitchell. Original series stars David Chokachi and Erika Eleniak are back to reprise their roles, though Pamela Anderson has already confirmed she will not be joining the series. As it stands, the Baywatch procedural could be Fox's best chance at finally replacing 9-1-1.

The series already has an IP that people will recognize, which could be a reason why Rescue HI-Surf failed to take off. Most first-responder shows come with a built-in audience of some kind, and if the revival is working with some of the same team that made the original a success, Baywatch has a great chance at also making this new iteration a hit too.

Fox has been searching for the right series to finally boost their ratings back to where they were during the 9-1-1 days. Baywatch is a perfect replacement because many people will tune into the premiere just to see how close it is to the original. Any fans of the show from back in the day will likely help Fox get impressive numbers to start out with. As long as the new show brings the drama and excitement that the original was known for, the Baywatch reboot will likely stick around for some time to come.

Obsession is the best horror movie I've seen in years. Stream Obsession on Peacock.

With the straight-laced couple's marriage on thin ice, Angela and Joe invite their more, uh, open-minded neighbors Piña, played by Penélope Cruz, and Hawk, played by Edward Norton, over for dinner. The evening unravels in hilarious ways, changing everyone's life. If you're a fan of smart, honest comedy, you will really like The Invite. Stream The Invite on HBO Max.

With Hokum, Director Damian McCarthy (Oddity, Caveat) carefully builds a suffocatingly creepy story around Adam Scott's portrayal of Ohm Bauman, a celebrity novelist and unmitigated jerk who travels to the isolated Bilberry Woods Hotel in Ireland to scatter the ashes of his parents and finish his book. Bauman soon learns that the lore of the hotel includes an ancient witch who feeds her victims to the creatures of hell, and she might be more than just a local legend. Hokum is a horror movie for fans of dreadful atmosphere and careful pacing instead of gore or jump-scares. Stream Hokum on Hulu.

With a title like this, it's not going to be a normal movie. Director Jane Schoenbrun’s I Saw the TV Glow and We're All Going to the World's Fair are two of the most fascinating, fiercely original horror movies of the last decade, and their third film follows in those strange footfalls. While it's technically a meta re-imagining of the slasher genre, Miasma goes way deeper than Scream ever could. It's a postmodern exploration of why the slasher genre's cocktail of sex, death, and subversion casts such a strong spell on interesting, weird people. Definitely see this movie. Stream Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma on Mubi.

When Golden Arm was released in 2021, not many people paid attention—with the pandemic in full swing, people didn't seem to have room for a quirky, indie comedy about a woman's quest to win the ladies' arm-wrestling championship—but it's a new age, and you should stream Golden Arm. It's sitting on a perfect score at Rotten Tomatoes, the movie's stars, Mary Holland and Betsy Sodaro, are charming and hilarious, and you can catch Golden Arm on Fandango, a free streaming service. What's not to love? Stream Golden Arm on Fandango or Prime Video.

In this crowd-pleasing sci-fi flick, Ryan Gosling stars as Ryland Grace, a middle school science teacher who is blasted into the firmament in a last-ditch effort to save the world. Grace is the only person on Earth who might know how to protect the sun from a cosmic infection that threatens all life, but he's definitely not an astronaut and doesn't see himself as a hero either. Will he rise to the occasion and learn something about his inner strength and resilience while saving us all from death? My money is on, "yeah, probably." Stream Project Hail Mary on MGM+, Prime Video, and Philo.

Hundreds of slasher movies have been released since Halloween came out in 1978, but none have surpassed the original. Michael Myers' expressionless visage and the synthesizer theme have become universally recognized cultural signifiers for "horror movie," and every shot in Halloween has been stolen countless times, but the movie is so good, it's still scary. Watch or re-watch Halloween now! Stream Halloween on Philo, AMC+, and Prime Video.

Directed by and starring Ben Affleck, Animals is a thriller that tells the story of Mark Kimball, a Los Angeles mayoral candidate whose son is kidnapped and held for ransom. Having spent every dime on his outsider campaign, Kimball is forced to turn to extreme methods to guarantee his son's safe return, even if it conflicts with his public persona as a man of the people. Animals is a taut, expertly directed movie that should more than satisfy fans of political thrillers. Stream Animals on Netflix.

StandBy mode was introduced with iOS 17, and it essentially turns the iPhone into a smart display when placed horizontally while charging.
